articles.title: Andy Burnham to publish all details of his dealings with Manchester City
articles.summary:
Move comes after criticism of remarks in support of football club’s owners following financial regulations breach ruling

Andy Burnham has said he will publish all details of his dealings…

blocks.text: Andy Burnham has said he will publish all details of his dealings with Manchester City in his previous mayoral role after his intervention in support of the football club’s owners raised eyebrows.

Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative party leader, had urged the prime minister to publish everything related to his work with the club as Greater Manchester mayor and the Liberal Democrats wrote to him asking him to release minutes of meetings and declare all hospitality gifts received from owners of Manchester City.
City have been found guilty of breaching Premier League financial regulations between 2009 and 2018. The club have maintained their innocence and appealed against the verdict.
Burnham said last month he would be “really concerned” if City’s Abu Dhabi owners sold the club after the finding, crediting them with being “a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester”.

Downing Street sought to clarify his comments afterwards, saying the prime minister was clear the judgment was serious and that where wrongdoing was established, those responsible should face the consequences.
Burnham said he would “put out there” everything he had done to work with the club’s owners as mayor in an interview with the Rest is Politics podcast to be released on Monday.
He said that “the football issues are different from the investment issues”.
“But I see now people trying to conflate these things. I’ve been asked by the leader of the opposition to publish details of my meetings, which I’m happy to do.
“I will quite clearly put out there everything that I have done working with them in my previous role as mayor of Greater Manchester.
“None of it is recent, actually, in terms of the meetings I had. I only had one significant meeting, actually, and that was in 2021. That is right and I will put that all out there.

“But the football issues, they are serious and have to be dealt with, and the process is independent and it has to run its course. But I think everybody should separate the investment issues because they’re not the same thing.”

The Premier League said an independent commission found City arranged “sham” commercial deals with a number of its sponsors during the period, which were part of a disguised funding scheme, whereby those companies were required to pay only a portion of the relevant sponsorship fees.
The commission found that the remainder was funded by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan’s Abu Dhabi United Group Investment and Development Ltd, which owned the club.

The shadow sports minister, Louie French, called for Burnham to also “come clean” about any meetings since becoming prime minister and urged Lisa Nandy, the secretary for digital, culture, media and sport, to respond to questions.

“The prime minister must publish every contact between his ministers, officials and Manchester City since he walked into No 10, the prime minister must also explain why he inappropriately intervened in this case, and Lisa Nandy must answer the questions I have put to her in full.”

articles.title: Air strikes kill dozens of gold miners on Sudan-Egypt border
articles.summary: A Sudan-based rights group said 72 people were killed in a remote, disputed area known for illegal gold mining.

image.caption: A UN report found that half of the gold mined in Sudan is smuggled out of the countryImage: Ashraf Shazly/AFP

blocks.text: At least 72 workers were killed in air strikes on a disputed border area between Sudan and Egypt that targeted artisanal gold miners, a human rights group said Sunday.
The attack, south of the remote Halayeb triangle, east of the River Nile, is the second of its kind this year.
It comes amid growing concern in Egypt over large-scale displacement from the three-and-a-half-year conflict in Sudan, which has spurred a cross-border exodus.
What do we know?
The Sudan-based Emergency Lawyers, a human rights and legal advocacy organization, said the attack occurred on Saturday in rugged and mountainous territory that it said lies within Sudan.
The Halayeb triangle, which is claimed by both Egypt and Sudan, is known for mining and the gold trade, along with other illicit goods and human trafficking.
The rights group accused the Egyptian air force of carrying out the strikes.
"The repeated attacks on the gold- and mineral-rich border regions reflect a desire by Egyptian authorities to expand and assert control over Sudan's natural resources," it claimed.
Egypt has yet to comment on the strikes, but has previously admitted conducting a "large-scale operation" against illegal gold mining within its borders.
Independent verification remains difficult because of the remote location.

blocks.caption: Child labor is widespread in Sudan's dangerous gold mining sectorImage: Interpol/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Death toll expected to rise

Sudan Doctors Network warned on Facebook of an expected increase in the number of casualties "due to the severity of some injuries and the difficulties in accessing medical care and essential services in the region."
One survivor told the AFP news agency there were thousands of people working at the remote site when it was hit.
"After the air strike, people scattered. Some people came to Al-Ansary [gold] market, others went in the other direction. That's why no one knows exactly how many were killed," he said.
Strikes tied to war's gold economy
Sudan's civil war between Abdel Fattah al-Burhan's military junta and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has killed more than 200,000 people and triggered a severe humanitarian crisis.
Despite backing Sudan's army chief al-Burhan, Egypt considers the war at its border a threat to its security.

The RSF has funded its operations by smuggling thousands of tons of gold from Sudan's Darfur and Kordofan regions. According to the UK-based think tank Chatham House, as much as 60% of unofficial gold exports end up in Egypt.
Sudan's civil war — the limits of humanitarian aid
In June, air strikes on mining sites in the same border area were followed by a large-scale Egyptian security operation.
Hundreds of people, including foreigners, were arrested, accused of illegal gold mining and smuggling.

articles.title: Orangutans released back into Borneo forest after devastating fires
articles.summary: Rescuers moved the apes after their habitats were threatened by intense wildfires over the summer.

blocks.text: Eight orangutans have been released back into the wild in Borneo after they were taken into captivity when their habitat was threatened by wildfires over the summer.
Three mothers, their three daughters and two adult males were freed in a reserve in the west of the island on Friday, International Animal Rescue Indonesia (Yiari) and the forestry ministry said.
Indonesian authorities rescued 46 orangutans from fires in August and September. Wildfires in the region are usual for the country's dry season but intensified this year.
The apes are critically endangered. Around 104,000 orangutans remain in Borneo and Sumatra, down from more than 230,000 a century ago, according to conservation group WWF.

While Indonesia is among many countries to grapple with wildfires each summer, this year's were more intense due to the El Niño ocean warming phenomenon, which makes weather patterns more volatile and intense.
Yiari CEO Karmele Llano Sanchez said relocating the eight orangutans to the reserve was a "necessary step" when their habitats became unsafe.
Among them was Mama Nopi and her offspring Nopi, Naufal and Nopan, who had been surviving in a coconut and rubber plantation before their rescue in early September, Yiari said.
Fires had incinerated the surrounding forestry, restricting their access to food and bringing them closer to humans.

articles.title: Who are the Ukrainian 'volunteers' under Russian command?
articles.summary: Russia has announced a battalion consisting of Ukrainian "volunteers." But veterans and former prisoners of war share very different accounts.

image.caption: Russian media reports say it has numerous military formations made up of former Ukrainian soldiersImage: Kaskad

blocks.text: Pavlo Oliynyk, 25, says he joined enemy forces to escape Russian captivity. Before his capture in the Donbas region in 2024, he was a senior lieutenant for Ukraine's armed forces.

As a prisoner of war (POW), he says he was electrocuted, beaten and psychologically tortured. So when he received the offer to join the Maksym Kryvonis battalion — named after a famous 17th-century Cossack commander — he accepted.
Oliynyk says he wanted to use this opportunity to reach the front lines, so he could escape to Ukrainian-controlled territory. DW was able to contact Oliynyk through his lawyer.
'Ukrainian volunteers' consist mostly of POWs

Reports of Russian combat units consisting of Ukrainian prisoners of war and former service members of Ukraine's armed forces began emerging in late 2022. Several detachments were initially formed and in August 2026, they were merged into the so-called "Ukrainian Volunteer Special Forces Brigade."

blocks.caption: Pavlo Oliynyk says he defected to Russian forces in order to escape captivityImage: Privatarchiv

blocks.text: Of the individual units, the Maksym Kryvonis battalion has perhaps drawn the most public attention for having evidently taken part in combat. Its true size is unknown — Russian media reports claim about 200 fighters while available footage only suggests several dozen.

An investigative team of the Ukrainian public broadcaster Suspilne has identified over 30 members and confirmed they are all former Ukrainian servicemen, captured by Russian forces between 2023 and 2024.
An 'imitation' of Russian legions fighting for Ukraine

Pavel Luzin, an expert for Russian foreign policy and defense at the Center for European Policy Analysis, believes these units are an "imitation" of the Russian Volunteer Corps and the Freedom of Russia Legion — units in the Ukrainian armed forces, consisting of Russian citizens — and an attempt by Moscow to distract from the fact that these units exist in the first place. Ukrainian intelligence services tend to agree.

"It bothers them that Russians would fight on Ukraine's side, but Ukrainians won't fight on Russia's side," Yevhen Shybalov, author and veteran of the war in Ukraine, told DW. He added that Russian troops have never tried to hide the fact that Russian volunteer units in Ukrainian ranks were the main reason Russian forces wanted to create Ukrainian units for their own ranks.
Just how voluntary are these combat units?
In 2025, the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) reported that 95% of the released Ukrainian POWs interviewed reported torture or ill-treatment during Russian captivity.

Bill Wiley, executive director of the NGO Commission for International Justice and Accountability, said the physical and psychological state of the returned combatants raises serious doubts that their recruitment was voluntary. Mykhailo Savva of the Center for Civil Liberties, a Kyiv-based human rights organization, points to the criminal procedures running against several of the battalion members, which he said indicates that these suggest the combatants had switched sides voluntarily.

But where to draw the line between voluntary and involuntary recruitment? The war veteran and human rights activist Maksym Butkevych, who spent 28 months as a prisoner of war, said the conditions in Russian captivity make that line hard to distinguish. On the one hand, he said, there is a constant atmosphere of pressure, and on the other hand, it's not implausible that some prisoners defected out of ideological proximity.
How were Ukrainian prisoners made to join Russian forces?

Butkevych told DW that between 2022 and 2023, all Ukrainian prisoners of war had received offers, "more or less persistently," to join the Russian army. In his case, he recounted, it was after he had been severely mistreated.
"They showed us they could do anything they wanted to us," he explained, "which was why we should agree to everything."

The veteran Shybalov reported similar experiences, speaking of attempts to force confessions of war crimes, or to recruit members for Russia's intelligence services. He told DW all prisoners were first interrogated and then made certain propositions under duress.

"You can torture people to get them to confess, but there comes the difficult moment when you need to give them a weapon," he said. "That's why it's more about psychological pressure, and forcing voluntary compliance."
Butkevych confirmed these accounts with his own tales. But neither veteran has ever met someone willing to join Russian units, they said.
What happens after conscription?
Oliynyk, from the Maksym Kryvonis battalion, said he initially turned down multiple bids to join Russian forces. He said he only accepted the fourth offer so he could flee.

He claimed he didn't sign official Defense Ministry paperwork, but a private contract with an individual offering military services. Afterwards, he said, he was brought to a room where he heard lectures and saw videos and photos he was later asked to retell.
Putin's foreign fighters
Control and mistreatment
Oliynyk said fellow service members in the Maksym Kryvonis battalion consisted both of those who had switched sides of their own volition, and those who had been forced.

In a video circulating online that appears to be of a trial in Ukraine, he also says former Ukrainian POWs in the unit were followed and guarded by mercenaries of the private Russian military company Redut. In the same video, he also speaks of beatings and torture, and receiving monthly wages in envelopes handed out by a member of Russia's military intelligence.

Oliynyk told DW he had been given a phone, but that he was too scared to call anyone in Ukraine because it was under constant surveillance. He denied having fought against Ukrainians, as he fled in March 2025 before his first deployment in the Donetsk province. After running across a field, he said he spent two days hiding from drones in basements and houses before making contact with Ukrainian fighters.
Now, Oliynyk has been in detention in Ukraine for nearly two years while authorities investigate possible treason. He has yet to be formally charged.
Sergey Nikitin contributed to this article, which originally appeared in Ukrainian.

articles.title: Trump and Rubio weigh firing Kimberly Guilfoyle after reports of improper conduct
articles.summary:
Senior official says president and US secretary of state are ‘extremely pissed off’ by conduct of US envoy to Greece

Donald Trump and Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, are considering…

blocks.text: Donald Trump and Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, are considering firing US ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after a series of reports alleging she has engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens.

A senior US official said Sunday that Trump and Rubio are “extremely pissed off” by Guilfoyle’s reported conduct and would likely decide on what action to take this week after Monday’s federal holiday.

The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations, said Rubio had been particularly angry, not least because he visited Athens just last week and Guilfoyle attended most, if not all, of his events and greeted him on his arrival with a bear hug as the allegations swirled.

In a series of stories, the Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill.
Guilfoyle has not addressed the reports directly, although her lawyer has said she did nothing wrong and the US embassy in Athens has tacitly expressed support for her.
After defending Guilfoyle following the first report, Rubio has declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. On Wednesday, Rubio said: “Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here.”

But after another report appeared late Wednesday, Rubio on Thursday before leaving Athens berated journalists for asking about the allegations saying he didn’t know if they were true and that he would not respond if he could not confirm.

“You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things,” Rubio said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart, looked on.
The official said that Rubio had grown increasingly frustrated as the reports multiplied.

A second US official, who also spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss personnel matters, said the state department’s inspector general is looking into the allegations, which first began surfacing in the Journal late last month and have since multiplied.

The second official could not say if a formal IG investigation had begun. Inspectors general often conduct informal inquiries into complaints against staffers and many times those inquiries do not result in a full-on investigation, which can result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal.
The state department has declined to comment on a potential IG investigation.

The top two Democrats on the House foreign affairs and Senate foreign relations committees, Representative Gregory Meeks of New York and Senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, as well as the ranking member on the House committee for oversight and government reform, Robert Garcia, Democrat of California, have already called for an investigation into Guilfoyle.

Since late September, the Journal has detailed numerous accounts of questionable conduct by Guilfoyle. Its first report said that she had told guests at a reception that the US could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company, and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings.

While Rubio was in Athens, the Journal reported – citing text messages – that Guilfoyle had asked a Trump donor and supporter to pay a $100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did.

The Journal then reported that Guilfoyle had been enraged about not being invited to a Greek-themed event at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, earlier this year and demanded to attend while boasting about luxury travel to France with energy company executives.

Another report, from the British tabloid The Daily Mail, said that Guilfoyle had alienated staff at the US embassy in Athens and had pushed the bounds of behavior appropriate for the top representative of the US government to Greece.
Guilfoyle is a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was once engaged to Trump’s son Donald Jr.

articles.title: Hurricane Simon hits Mexico's Pacific coast, slamming towns and resorts
articles.summary: Hurricane Simon was pounding Mexico's Pacific coast as a Category 4 storm on Sunday, its eye remaining just offshore as its most powerful winds and rain slammed people living between the Sierra Madre…

image.caption: A child wades through a flooded street as Hurricane Simon approaches Mexico's Pacific coast, bringing heavy rain and strong winds to Manzanillo, Mexico, on Sunday. (Daniel Becerril/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·Updated

Hurricane Simon was pounding Mexico's Pacific coast as a Category 4 storm on Sunday, its eye remaining just offshore as its most powerful winds and rain slammed people living between the Sierra Madre and the ocean.
Hurricane specialist says 'life-threatening' storm surge expected

Simon's eye was moving northward just off the coast, and forecasters at the U.S. National Hurricane Center said it's not clear if it will make landfall. This could mean Simon maintains its extremely dangerous strength, sustaining winds of 240 km/h.

That's not good news for people in the Puerto Vallarta area, a popular destination for Canadian tourists. Just inland and uphill from the resort areas, many Mexicans live in communities where housing might not stand up to the storm.

At daybreak, Simon was centered about 175 kilometres south-southeast of Cabo Corrientes, and moving north-northwest at a relatively slow eight km/h. A senior Hurricane Center specialist, Phillippe Pappin, said this westernmost tip of mainland Mexico was the most likely place for landfall.
"Simon is very close to the coast of Mexico this morning," Pappin told The Associated Press on Sunday.
"We're expecting catastrophic wind and life-threatening storm surge impacts along that west central coast of Mexico where the hurricane warning is currently in effect," Pappin said.

"They're also getting very heavy rainfall associated with the storm that's likely going to produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides in areas of higher terrain along the Mexican coastline, and there will be significant swells."

items: Category 4 Hurricane Simon barrels toward Mexico
Hurricane Simon forecast to get much stronger as it heads to Mexico's Pacific Coast

blocks.text: As for predicting whether or not Simon will make landfall, "it's a little tricky right now" to forecast, since the eye "is basically moving very close or parallel to the coast currently," Pappin said. But he predicted that Cabo Corrientes is the area most likely to get a direct hit from the system on Sunday.
Waves hit the shore in Manzanillo on Sunday. (Daniel Becerril/Reuters)
Heavy rainfall elsewhere

Meanwhile, the hurricane was dumping rain over parts of southwestern Mexico. It could bring 25 to 50 centimetres of rain in many places, with some areas in the states of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco receiving up to 76 centimetres. "This rainfall will produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain," the centre warned.

Jalisco state suspended classes on Friday and Monday in 22 coastal municipalities and began evacuating people from at-risk areas while asking the tourism sector to make sure workers as well as visitors are fully accommodated in shelters or safe zones.
On Saturday, just ahead of the worst weather, convenience stores, hotels and other businesses in Puerto Vallarta were boarding up their windows.
A man removes water from a building in Manzanillo on Sunday. (Daniel Becerril/Reuters)

The hurricane centre expected a dangerous storm surge along the immediate coast near and to the east of where the centre makes landfall. The agency warned that near the coast, large and destructive waves will accompany the surge.
Canadian tourist Ed Currie, who, along with his wife, still has five more days to enjoy Puerto Vallarta, said the hurricane had not yet affected his plans.
"Just stay in the hotel and look out the window hopefully," he said of what the couple would do. "I just don't know what to expect."

articles.title: Children among at least 139 dead after migrant boat capsizes off Djibouti coast
articles.summary: At least 139 people, including children, have died after a boat carrying more than 300 migrants capsized off the coast of Djibouti in East Africa, the International Organization for Migration said…

image.caption: This image provided by the International Organization for Migration shows a boat after it capsized near Guhere, Djibouti, on Saturday. (Alexandre Coissac/International Organization for Migration/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

At least 139 people, including children, have died after a boat carrying more than 300 migrants capsized off the coast of Djibouti in East Africa, the International Organization for Migration said Sunday.
Toll only includes those buried by authorities, says UN migration agency

That number only includes those buried by authorities in Djibouti. Others have been buried by the migrants themselves, but they won't be added to the official count until authorities can verify the bodies, Alexandre Coissac, IOM chief of mission in Djibouti, told The Associated Press.
"What is terrible is that they were buried with no names, in a common grave, like in a war situation," Coissac said. "They all have a mother, a father, and we may never learn what happened."
Coissac said the migrants boarded the ship in the evening of Oct. 8 and that it sank very soon after, close to the shore, "mainly because it was overcrowded."
"The local authorities did their best," Coissac said, "but they were overwhelmed with all the bodies that kept coming at once towards the shore."
He said authorities were bringing the surviving migrants to the IOM rescue centre in Obock where they would receive medical assistance after swallowing sea water, and psychological support.
A pair of trousers believed to belong to a migrant lies on the shore near Guhere. (Kennedy Omondi Okoth/International Organization for Migration/Reuters)
"They're all in a state of shock," said Coissac, who visited the area of the shipwreck Saturday. "I tried to talk to some of them, but it's very difficult."

Some of the migrants in the IOM centre are already aware that their family members died during the shipwreck. Others were given access to phones to call loved ones back home to notify them they are alive.

At least 84 people remained missing in one of the deadliest shipwrecks yet on the popular but perilous crossing from the Horn of Africa to the Arabian Peninsula, where many migrants seek work in rich Gulf nations.

The death toll from the #Djibouti shipwreck has risen to 139, with 84 people still missing. As search and recovery efforts continue, IOM is providing emergency assistance to survivors. Every life lost is one too many. Read the latest updates here: https://t.co/LJjeAtSer2 https://t.co/VXfiv3TeFA—UNmigration
The boat was travelling from Djibouti to Yemen when it capsized on Thursday night or Friday morning, according to the IOM. More than 80 people survived, all of them Ethiopian nationals, it said.
The Geneva-based UN migration agency said the vessel had 305 people on board and warned that the death toll could still rise.
Personal items likely belonging to the migrants, including shoes, were seen on a beach in a video shared by IOM. Rescue work continued as fears grew for the missing.
'Safe and legal pathways save lives'

Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa travel every year through Djibouti and across the Bab el-Mandeb Strait toward Gulf countries in search of safety and economic opportunities, the IOM said in its statement.
That movement has continued despite newly escalating fighting in Yemen, on the other side of the strait.
"This is a devastating loss of life," said Coissac. "This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities."
Members of the International Organization for Migration receive migrants near Guhere. (Kennedy Omondi Okoth/International Organization for Migration/Reuters)

In recent weeks, at least 2,000 Yemenis have received aid in Djibouti as the fighting has escalated in Yemen between the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government and Iran-backed Houthi rebels.

That's the opposite direction from the movement of the migrants who died in the shipwreck and the typical migration patterns of recent years: the tens of thousands who cross from eastern Africa toward Yemen each year have typically been looking for work in places like Saudi Arabia.

blocks.text: Over 900 migrants died or went missing along the route last year, according to IOM's Missing Migrants Project.

"No one gets into a boat like that unless they believe there is no other safe way," IOM director general Amy Pope said. "We cannot keep treating these deaths as normal. Safe and legal pathways save lives. I am asking governments and donors to act before the next boat goes down."

articles.title: Poland detains man suspected of planning assassination of PM Tusk

blocks.text: Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said a man accused of plotting an assassination attack against him and his defence minister has been detained.
The interior ministry earlier reported that police had received credible information about possible attacks against Tusk and Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz.
Security services convened a special meeting on Sunday after receiving information about the planned attacks, with a spokesman saying officials were treating the threat as "deadly serious".
Tusk thanked the police for "swift and decisive action" in arresting the suspect.
The suspect was arrested in the Lower Silesia region and is a Polish national, Jacek Dobrzynski, a spokesman for the Special Services Coordinator told local media.
"In this case we are talking about a strong likelihood that these threats could actually be carried out," he said.

The plan was uncovered when an email with information about the potential attack was forwarded to police by the State Protection Service, which is responsible for ministers' security, Interior Ministry spokeswoman Karolina Galecka said.
Tusk has been Polish prime minister since 2023 after previously holding the office from 2007 to 2014.
He served as president of the European Council from 2014 to 2019.

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed: Democrats must ‘win by massive numbers’ to fend off Trump election denial
articles.summary:
Democratic Senate candidate’s remarks come as Trump has long baselessly claimed his 2020 election loss was stolen

Democrats must…

blocks.text: Democrats must “win by massive numbers” during November’s federal midterm elections because Donald Trump and his Republican allies are bound to try to sow doubt about the integrity of the results, Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan said on Sunday.

El-Sayed’s comments on NBC’s Meet the Press came with the Democrats favored to win control of the House of Representatives during the 3 November midterms – and polls show that the party could also win Senate seats in states that traditionally elect Republicans and gain a majority there, too.
Meanwhile, Trump has long baselessly maintained that the 2020 presidential election which he lost as an incumbent to Joe Biden was stolen by fraudsters.
He also gave a primetime speech in July in which he made unverified claims about Chinese interference in the election, and he fired members of an independent federal election commission.

When asked later by a rightwing broadcaster whether the president might declare a national security emergency pertaining to elections for the midterms, Trump ignited alarm among some observers by replying: “Let me just say, stranger things have happened, OK?”
The New York Times, meanwhile, reported that Trump had cast doubt on elections on 440 days of his second presidency, which began in early 2025.

As such, on NBC’s Meet the Press Sunday, El-Sayed was asked whether Democrats needed to turn out in such numbers in November that the election would be “too big to rig” – as it had recently been put by former vice-president Kamala Harris, who lost the 2024 White House election to Trump.
“Donald Trump has already threatened to do what he did in 2020, which is deny the outcomes of an election,” El-Sayed said. “So, yes, we have to win by massive numbers.”
The Cook Political Report revised its predictions on Tuesday and declared that “A Senate Majority is Squarely in Democrats’ Sights”.
A recent New York Times and Siena University poll found Democratic Senate candidates leading in Alaska, Ohio and Texas, states that Trump won by double digits in 2024.
The poll showed El-Sayed leading Republican candidate Mike Rogers by five points.

El-Sayed on Sunday’s Meet the Press alluded to how Rogers had also claimed that a 2024 US Senate election which he lost to Elissa Slotkin, a Democrat, was stolen from him – after first having conceded the race.
Rogers in November 2025 was reported to have said at events that a single van carrying fraudulent ballots in Detroit cost him the race against Slotkin.
“The guy … I’m running against insinuates that he didn’t actually lose,” El-Sayed said to Kristen Welker. “That’s the guy I’m running against right now.”

articles.title: Volkswagen boss backs EU plan to boost domestic European industry
articles.summary:
Oliver Blume says ‘Made in Europe’ rules to counter rapid rise of lower-price Chinese brands ‘must reward real value creation’

The boss of Volkswagen has backed EU proposals to boost its…

blocks.text: The boss of Volkswagen has backed EU proposals to boost its domestic industry, arguing European carmakers need to be able to “compete under comparable conditions” with Chinese rivals.
Oliver Blume said “Made in Europe” rules from the EU “must reward real value creation in Europe”, speaking in Paris before the motor show this week.

The rules are aimed at countering the rapid rise of Chinese brands in Europe in the automotive sector and other important manufacturing industries. Lower-priced Chinese manufacturers have prompted a crisis in several industries.

Volkswagen is among the most-affected European companies. Germany’s biggest carmaker has launched a brutal plan to cut as many as 100,000 jobs. Blume said it was the “largest transformation programme in its history”.

The proposals for the Made in Europe rules, formally known as the Industrial Accelerator Act, would limit subsidies and public procurement to products with a large proportion of their materials and manufacturing coming from within the EU.

Blume listed a litany of challenges facing European carmakers, saying: “Europe is under enormous competitive pressure.” These included: high energy costs; lower demand as consumers struggle with high inflation; the need to be quicker to develop cars; and intense competition from China.
On Friday, the EU said it had reached a landmark deal with China to “halve” its sales of hybrid cars in the bloc amid fears surging sales could kill off parts of the European car industry.
Blume said Germany’s carmakers were happy to compete with Chinese rivals, but said the EU should try to reward businesses with significant European footprints.
“Companies that invest and develop in Europe must see a clear benefit,” he said.
Referring to Chinese companies, he added: “Those who sell here should compete under comparable conditions and create jobs and value here in Europe, too.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: The new all-electric ID Tiguan. Photograph: Volkswagen AG

blocks.text: Blume added: “We believe in open markets, but openness also means standing up for our own interests in Europe. Because a strong industrial base means more than economic success. It protects technological independence.”
Volkswagen is exhibiting at the Paris show for the first time in 20 years. Blume emphasised the “close ties between France and Germany”, while hosting the French industry minister, Sébastian Martin.
Arno Antlitz, VW’s chief financial officer, said the job cuts were necessary to “increase our economic power” by increasing profitability and allowing it to defend its “home turf”.

The company is cutting the number of models it offers worldwide from 150 to 75 across brands including Audi and Škoda. It hopes the move will reduce complexity in its factories and for dealers, cutting the cost of each vehicle it makes.
On Sunday, it revealed the production version of its ID Tiguan, an electric edition of its bestselling family SUV.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia's Riyadh airport hit by second Houthi strike in two days
articles.summary: The Yemeni group says it carried out attacks that killed 13 people over the weekend and targeted two airports and oil facilities.

blocks.text: An international airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh has been hit by a second strike in as many days, officials have said.

A Saudi military spokesman said a projectile had hit King Khalid International Airport on Sunday, causing a fire in one of its passenger halls. Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said there had been injuries.
It comes a day after a strike on the same airport killed 13 people and injured 308 others, following similar strikes earlier this week.
The Houthis in Yemen said they were behind the attacks and warned airlines and passengers against using Saudi Arabian airports and airspace.
The group said they had targeted the airport with a mix of ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as drones in the past 24 hours.
They also attacked oil facilities and Dammam airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, their military spokesman Brig Gen Yahya Saree said.
He vowed to continue the "escalating operations deep inside Saudi Arabia", warning that all Saudi airports were potential targets apart from those in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.
The Houthis have said they are targeting Saudi Arabia over its support for government forces in Yemen's civil war, as well as an air strike on the airport in Sanaa.

On Sunday Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition, said air defences had intercepted a missile near the airport in Riyadh, while authorities were dealing with the fire caused by an "unknown projectile" that hit Passenger Hall No 4.

US President Donald Trump has said the US would "make a decision" and "move very quickly" on whether to strike the Houthis, while UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting suggested the UK could "potentially" provide more support for Saudi Arabia.

articles.title: Most Pinoys open to discussing mental health woes – SWS
articles.summary: A large majority of Filipinos are open to discussing mental health challenges to help other people understand the issue, a recent survey by Social Weather Stations (SWS) showed.

blocks.text: October 12, 2026 | 12:00am
The survey, conducted from Sept. 21 to 27, found that 72 percent of the respondents agreed to the statement: “Being open to talk about mental health challenges help people understand them.”
The STAR / Ryan Baldemor
MANILA, Philippines — A large majority of Filipinos are open to discussing mental health challenges to help other people understand the issue, a recent survey by Social Weather Stations (SWS) showed.
Only 15 percent disagreed with the statement, while 13 percent were undecided.
The survey also asked respondents if they agree to the statement: “Sharing my own mental health experiences helps other people feel like they are not alone.”
Seventy-eight percent of the respondents agreed, while the remaining 22 percent were evenly divided among those disagreed and were undecided.
The survey found that only 18 percent of the respondents rated their mental health as “excellent,” slightly down from 20 percent last year.
Twelve percent said it was “very good” (almost similar to 12 percent last year), while 31 percent said it was “good” (from 28 percent).
A large chunk of respondents self-assessed their mental health as “fair” (38 percent, similar to last year), while two percent described it as “poor” (from one percent).
Although the results of the mental health self-assessment poll were almost similar to last year, SWS data showed that it was significantly different from a similar survey in 2021.
At the time, only 17 percent rated their mental health as “fair,” with more than half describing it as “excellent” (24 percent), “very good’ (29 percent) or “good” (29 percent).

A similar poll conducted the year prior, at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, resulted in the highest percentage of respondents – eight percent – rating their mental health as “poor.” Almost half or 45 percent said their mental health was “fair” at the time.
The latest survey also asked respondents who would they first approach in times of mental health struggle.
While parents remained the top answer, results showed that they dropped from being the first choice of the respondents from 53 percent last year to just 29 percent.
Twenty-seven percent said they would approach their partner (similar to last year), while 11 percent said siblings (up from 10 percent).
The survey showed a significant increase among those who would approach local government units (11 percent, from two percent) and mental health professions (10 percent, from four percent).

articles.title: Probe sought on Chinese remittances to Cale88
articles.summary: Reports that Chinese firms remitted P319 million to a company linked to Manases Carpio, Vice President Sara Duterte’s husband, warrant a “full-blown national security…

blocks.text: October 12, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Reports that Chinese firms remitted P319 million to a company linked to Manases Carpio, Vice President Sara Duterte’s husband, warrant a “full-blown national security investigation,” according to Batangas Rep. Gerville Luistro, lead prosecutor of the House of Representatives.
Luistro made the remark after an Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) report exposed remittances from China to Cale88 Foods Corp., a firm linked to Carpio, who held a substantial 47.5 percent stake.

“I honestly believe this is something that should be looked into and investigated, especially since the National Security Council had acknowledged the sensitivity of this issue concerning all Filipinos who have remittances from China,” she explained.
Luistro was referring to financial records presented during Duterte’s impeachment trial showing that Cale88 Foods Corp. received P319.33 million in remittances from mainland China and Hong Kong.

AMLC executive director lawyer Ronel Buenaventura confirmed the transactions in the Senate impeachment court during his testimony last Oct. 5, based on covered and suspicious transaction reports submitted by banks and financial institutions.
The AMLC records showed that P319.33 million went into Cale88’s corporate accounts, not directly into the personal accounts of Duterte or Carpio.
“Money from China poured into a food manufacturing company of her (Duterte’s) husband,” private prosecutor Mae Divinagracia said, as she conducted a direct examination on the AMLC executive.

“Their companies moved billions more,” Divinagracia said further. The prosecutor stated that from 2022 to 2025, nearly P4.5 billion was recorded as entering and leaving 15 corporations in which Duterte and Carpio allegedly had business interests.

In her offer of testimony, she told the court that Cale88 Foods Corp. was established in 2021 and that Carpio, Duterte’s husband, holds 47.5 percent of its shares. The prosecutor said three of the remittances had been reported by a bank as suspicious.
Luistro said the transactions should be examined against the backdrop of continuing tensions between the Philippines and China in the West Philippine Sea.

The NSC earlier announced that it would examine the reported foreign financial inflows and coordinate with intelligence and investigative agencies to determine whether they posed national security risks.

The allegation linking Vice President Duterte to Chinese funds is “a threat at the highest level to the Republic,” President Marcos said yesterday, as he denied involvement in supposed efforts to besmirch her name.

“That now rises to a national security issue if true. If it is true, it is a national security issue. That’s why the DND (Department of National Defense) responded and they said, we have to look into this. That’s right. That’s part of their duty because national security is involved if it is true,” the President said.
“Nothing would make me happier than proof that it is not true. Then it’s one less thing that I have to worry about. But if it is true, it is a threat at the highest level to the Republic.”

Meanwhile, Carpio maintained the credit card expenses discussed during the impeachment trial were personal expenditures paid for with his own money, insisting the Vice President had no involvement in the transactions and no public funds were used. — Alexis Romero

articles.title: Prosecutors rest impeachment case vs VP Sara
articles.summary: To expedite the long-drawn proceedings, the House prosecution team has decided to conclude its presentation of evidence against Vice President Sara Duterte before the Senate impeachment court today.

blocks.text: October 12, 2026 | 12:00am
Vice President Sara Duterte arrives before the start of the impeachment trial at the Senate of the Philippines in Pasay, Metro Manila on July 7, 2026.
Noel Celis, pool / AFP

MANILA, Philippines — To expedite the long-drawn proceedings, the House prosecution team has decided to conclude its presentation of evidence against Vice President Sara Duterte before the Senate impeachment court today.

House lead prosecutor Rep. Gerville Luistro said this has been the consensus of both the public and private assigned prosecutors handling all the Articles of Impeachment, with the remaining bribery charge to be forwarded to the Office of the Ombudsman under Jesus Crispin Remulla.

“From the conclusion of the testimony of the expert witness we wish to seek the guidance of the impeachment court as to when we will be filing the formal offer of exhibits,” Luistro said, acknowledging that the bank records’ testimony is quite lengthy.
Luistro also confirmed the decision to forgo the bribery charge, which was done to expedite the proceedings and come to its final conclusion at the soonest time possible.

When the Senate impeachment court resumes its hearing today, Luistro said that financial analyst expert lawyer Alexander Cabrera will once again take the witness stand for the cross-examination to be conducted by the defense panel. This will be followed by a redirect examination by the prosecution and a re-cross by the defense, if necessary.

The prosecution has earlier filed a manifestation before the Senate impeachment court that Cabrera will be its last witness and it will no longer be presenting evidence on Article III, or the bribery charge where officials of the Department of Education were supposed to testify.

Luistro added the prosecution will also be seeking guidance from the court if it will push through with the calling of additional witnesses, particularly on Impeachment Article I or the allegation that Duterte misused P612.5 million in confidential funds allocated to the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and the Department of Education (DepEd), which used to be headed by Duterte.
Bribery raps

The House prosecution panel also sought to allay concerns over its decision to drop the bribery charge against Duterte, saying the allegations could still be referred to the ombudsman or the Department of Justice for possible investigation.
Luistro said the withdrawal of the charge, handled by fellow prosecutor Rep. Jonathan Keith Flores, would not prevent authorities from pursuing the allegations through separate legal proceedings.

“Please don’t lose hope in the bribery charge because even if we have already manifested that this is withdrawn as shared already by honorable Flores, there are proper agencies or offices which have jurisdiction over this case,” said Luistro, chairperson of the House committee on justice.
The charge involved allegations that Vice President Duterte gave money to DepEd officials to influence procurement decisions during her term as education secretary.
Among the allegations was former DepEd undersecretary Gloria Mercado’s account of receiving nine envelopes containing P50,000 each.

articles.title: ‘Power rate hikes during El Niño must not burden families’
articles.summary: Sen. Erwin Tulfo has warned power companies against imposing unjustified rate hikes and delivering substandard service during the impending “super El Niño.”

blocks.text: October 12, 2026 | 12:00am
Linemen install new transformers on an electric post along United Nations Avenue in Manila on March 22, 2026.
The Philippine STAR / Ryan Baldemor
MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Erwin Tulfo has warned power companies against imposing unjustified rate hikes and delivering substandard service during the impending “super El Niño.”

The warning from the Senate committee on energy chairman follows advisories from the Department of Energy (DOE) and distribution utilities regarding expected electricity price spikes and rolling blackouts.

“While rate adjustments are expected due to supply and demand dynamics, any price increase must remain fair and reasonable. It should not worsen the financial burden already felt by Filipino families on a daily basis,” Tulfo said.
“I will not hesitate to exercise oversight functions if power generation companies or distribution utilities exploit the climate crisis to maximize profits,” he added.
Tulfo urged the DOE and Energy Regulatory Commission to implement safeguards ensuring stable supply and preventing artificial shortages meant to justify price spikes.

While he acknowledged the House of Representatives’ approval of funding for sitio electrification in the 2027 General Appropriations bill, Tulfo said this is insufficient without executive agencies coordinating on the ground.
State weather forecasters said El Niño will intensify between September to December and persist through the first half of 2027.

articles.title: House breaks for Undas, sessions resume November 9
articles.summary: The House of Representatives will take a nearly month-long Undas break starting today after the plenary approves on third and final reading the P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027, which the…

blocks.text: October 12, 2026 | 12:00am
Workers do renovation works around the House of Representatives within the Batasang Pambansa Complex in Quezon City on July 3, 2024.
STAR / Miguel De Guzman

MANILA, Philippines — The House of Representatives will take a nearly month-long Undas break starting today after the plenary approves on third and final reading the P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027, which the Senate will also deliberate on.

The lower chamber is expected to pass House Bill 10858 or the General Appropriations Bill (GAB) for 2027 that the appropriations committee chaired by Rep. Mikaela Suansing has been scrutinizing since mid-August.
Both the Senate and House will resume legislative sessions on Nov. 9.

The nine-day plenary debates on the Marcos administration’s proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027 have been concluded by the House in late September, and the spending measure was passed on second reading last week.

“There are very many advocacies that we are pushing in the House, but the most important here is what we have been doing in the national budget. We are making sure that each and every centavo, which is hard-earned by our taxpayers, are allocated properly and spent judiciously,” Speaker Faustino Dy III said.
Meanwhile, Suansing made assurances there will be additional safeguards as they crafted the 2027 GAB, particularly on the rules and standards governing the use and evaluation of funds.
The Department of Education still had the lion’s share in the spending measure, along with the Department of Health, as government tries to strengthen the health care system.

The House’s commitment is reflected in the retention of the P1.107-trillion allocation for the education sector under the National Expenditure Program, which remains at the same level in the House GAB approved on second reading.

Realignments were made within the sector, funneling funds from programs with billions of pesos in unutilized appropriations toward priority programs requiring more urgent support, without any reduction in the overall education budget.
A total of P10.055 billion in additional allocations was directed toward education programs, supporting school safety, inclusive learning, academic recovery and access to quality tertiary education.
Among the approved amendments is support for students pursuing higher education, including an additional P2.10 billion for the Tertiary Education Subsidy.
The House also approved a P12.23-billion increase in the health sector’s budget, raising its allocation from P346.59 billion under the NEP to P358.82 billion under the GAB approved on second reading.

MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Panfilo Lacson dared Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano to name the individuals he allegedly threatened over the ongoing probe into anomalous infrastructure projects and reclamation activities in Taguig City.
In a post on X, Lacson responded to Cayetano’s Facebook livestream, where the minority leader claimed he received feelers that parties were being pressured to admit to irregularities in Taguig.
“Spinning tales betrays panic, but like guilt, it will never go away,” Lacson said.
“Sen. Cayetano should name the ‘individuals’ he alleged I threatened, so I can properly address this new issue point by point,” he added.

Lacson previously submitted at least 45 case studies to the Office of the Ombudsman detailing alleged anomalies in flood control infrastructure projects in Taguig, prompting a fact-finding investigation.
He also released a video from an inspection team documenting continued illegal reclamation on the Taguig side of Laguna Lake.

Recalling an earlier exchange on Sept. 3, Lacson dismissed Cayetano’s claims of a political demolition job: “PATHETIC. Imagine someone ‘quacking’ on FB Live with accusations of politically motivated demolition job, fake news and trial by publicity and at the same time ‘quaking in his boots’ every time each piece of evidence of corruption in his turf unfolds before his eyes.”
The probe into reclamation projects in Taguig comes amid the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

articles.title: ICC, members push back vs US sanctions
articles.summary: The International Criminal Court (ICC) and some of its member countries have pushed back against the institutional sanction imposed by the United States government against the tribunal.

blocks.text: October 12, 2026 | 12:00am
This photograph taken on March 14, 2025 shows the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague.
AFP / Nicolas Tucat

MANILA, Philippines — The International Criminal Court (ICC) and some of its member countries have pushed back against the institutional sanction imposed by the United States government against the tribunal.
In a statement, the ICC described the sanctions as an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the Court from doing what it was created to do.

“This measure targets an independent judicial institution, created by treaty and entrusted by 125 States Parties with investigating and prosecuting genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression,” the tribunal said in a statement delivered by its president, Tomoko Akane.
“It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law,” it added.
The US government imposed the sanction hours after a former judge, Navi Pillay, was announced as this year’s Nobel Peace Prize winner.
According to the US State Department, the institutional sanction on the ICC would prevent US persons or those within the country from making any contribution or providing support to the tribunal.

The sanction is intended to “ban transactions” and cut off resources that could impact the tribunal’s operations. It follows the individuals sanctions imposed by the US against 13 judges and prosecutors.
Despite the sanctions, Akane said the court will continue to operate and fulfill its functions.

“The Court will continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence, for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes,” she said.
The ICC has urged members to continue taking concrete actions to assist the institution.

“No one should be punished for serving the cause of justice. History will judge this moment. Future generations, and above all the victims of mass atrocities, will ask how we responded when an institution created to protect them came under attack,” it said.
In a separate statement, Bureau of the Assembly of State Parties said it regrets the sanctions imposed by the US government.

“The escalation in unprecedented use of coercive measures is a regrettable attempt to impede the Court and its personnel in the exercise of their independent judicial functions. Such actions aim to directly challenge an international legal institution painstakingly built to ensure that accountability, not impunity, prevails,” it said.

Foreign ministers of the United Kingdom, Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands issued a joint statement reaffirming the support of their respective countries to the tribunal.

articles.title: Trump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war as Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’
articles.summary: Ukrainian president earlier rejected US call for Kyiv to stop bombing oil refineries, saying Moscow must first end attacks on energy infrastructure

blocks.text: Donald Trump has announced an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia, apparently without consulting Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said the deal to stop long-range attacks was “news to me”.

In a social media post, the US president claimed the two sides had reached an agreement. “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on Truth Social.

He offered no further details. Zelenskyy said he was surprised by the announcement but would agree to it if Vladimir Putin did the same. “If President Trump negotiated it with Putin – please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready and we will accept it,” the Ukrainian president told the Axios website.

Earlier, Zelenskyy rebuffed Trump’s demand made on Saturday that Kyiv stop bombing Russian oil refineries. Zelenskyy said Moscow had to first halt its own “brutal” attacks on his country’s energy infrastructure.

Any deal to end long-range drone strikes by Ukraine on targets inside Russia would have to be “reciprocal”, he said. It should be backed by “real guarantees” – meaning punitive measures against Moscow from Ukraine’s allies, including the US.

blocks.caption: The aftermath on Sunday of a Russian strike on Kharkiv that hit residential homes. Photograph: Vyacheslav Madiyevskyy/Reuters

blocks.text: This is not the first time Trump has announced an energy ceasefire deal. He made the same claim in September, which turned out to be untrue. Ukrainian officials said Russia was still bombing Ukraine on Sunday, with several energy sites damaged.

The fast-moving row between Washington and Kyiv began on Friday when Trump announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports. He said the move would reduce global and domestic fuel prices before next month’s US midterm elections.

A furious Zelenskyy called the decision “weak” and said it would generate “billions” in extra revenue for Putin, enabling him to wage war “even more intensely”. An equally irate Trump said Zelenskyy should “damn well stop” hitting Russian refineries. Ukraine needed a “new leader”, he said on Saturday.

Responding to Trump, Zelenskyy said it was up to Ukrainians to choose “one or another leader”. He told ABC News he was willing to accept Trump’s demands and to organise elections, but only if Putin agreed to a “total” 60-day ceasefire.
The bitter public feud is the most serious between the US and Ukraine since last year, when Trump berated Zelenskyy in the Oval Office.

The New York Times has reported that US officials have offered the Kremlin lucrative economic incentives in exchange for a ceasefire. They reportedly include releasing billions in Russian sovereign assets that are frozen. The Trump administration also revisited a plan to sell parts of Russia’s energy company, Lukoil. The multibillion deal would benefit Middle Eastern investors, the paper reported, some with “business ties” to US negotiators.

blocks.caption: Medics help a woman injured in a Russian attack on a residential area in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine on Saturday after overnight strikes.  Photograph: Daryna Naumova/EPA

blocks.text: On Saturday, Trump berated Zelenskyy and said he had refused to make a deal to end the fighting. In response, Ukraine’s president laid the blame for Europe’s biggest war since 1945 on “Russia and Russia alone”. “It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but Putin does not want to do so,” he said.

Ukrainian officials point out that the White House is demanding Kyiv give up its most effective weapon, without demanding any corresponding concessions from Russia. In recent weeks, Kyiv has dealt a major blow to Russia’s economy, striking oil complexes, warehouses and datacentres.

Russia’s own bombing campaign has been relentless. On Saturday it killed 23 people in the city of Zaporizhzhia, including four children, and hit a five-storey apartment block in the frontline town of Sloviansk. Zelenskyy said Moscow’s aerial campaign involved thousands of aerial bombs and jet-powered drones. It continued “unabated”, he said.
after newsletter promotion

The head of Ukraine’s foreign affairs committee, Oleksandr Merezhko, said Trump’s “bullying” demand for Zelenskyy to quit had strengthened him at home “paradoxically”, after recent damaging corruption scandals. “Putin’s plan is to decapitate Zelenskyy and remove him as a wartime leader. Trump is siding with Putin,” Merezhko said.

He added: “I’m afraid that behind this situation is Trump’s worldview. He wants to do business with Putin. For him, Ukraine seems like an obstacle to be removed. Both Trump and Putin wish to pressure us into capitulation.”
Referring to the notorious 1939 agreement between Nazi Germany and the USSR, Merezhko said: “We are moving to a new Molotov-Ribbentrop pact and to a world of strongmen and spheres of influence.”

Merezhko said Ukraine would continue to destroy enemy oil refineries, against US wishes, because they funded Russia’s war machine and acknowledged that a cutoff of US intelligence sharing with Kyiv – threatened by the Trump administration – would “blind” Ukraine’s air defence systems. “This would be an act of complicity with Putin’s genocide. It would mean more dead civilians and dead children,” he said.

Ukrainian negotiators had been meeting in Florida with their American counterparts, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, when Trump announced the US was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel. Blindsided, the Ukrainians went home early. “It felt like a trap,” one stunned Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent newspaper.

On Saturday, Zelenskyy shored up support in a series of conversations with key European allies including the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, and the Finnish president, Alexander Stubb. Downing Street said Burnham recognised the last 24 hours had been “difficult” for Ukraine and “reiterated his complete solidarity”.

Downing Street said the two leaders agreed “to maintain pressure on Russia” and to strengthen the sanctions regime, despite Trump’s efforts to the contrary. “Russia should agree to an immediate energy ceasefire, ending its brutal strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure and its attacks on shipping in the Black Sea,” a statement added.

Speaking over the weekend, Zelenskyy said Trump’s decision empowered Putin and gave him “extra money for the war”, running into millions and “perhaps billions”. “It is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should act. And, in my view, it is a weak decision,” he said.

articles.title: Trump’s deal with Putin will have little impact on US diesel prices, experts say
articles.summary: Analysts say fuel will take weeks to ship and quantity is too small to affect prices, while full deal is unlikely to be met given damage to Russian refineries

blocks.text: Donald Trump’s deal with Vladimir Putin to temporarily lift sanctions on US imports of Russian diesel will have little “meaningful” effect on motorists and businesses in the US and overseas, energy and foreign policy analysts have predicted.

The US president infuriated Volodymyr Zelenskyy when he announced the deal on Friday, writing on Truth Social that the agreement with his Russia counterpart to supply millions of tonnes of diesel was essential to reduce fuel prices in the US, which have soared after his decision to go to war against Iran.

The package announced by Trump involves 300,000 tonnes of diesel released immediately “to the American and global marketplace” followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and a further 1m tonnes after that. The 300,000 figure equates to about three-quarters of what the US would use in a day, according to calculations using figures from the US Energy Information Administration.

“Diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my greatest priority,” Trump posted.

However, experts suggested that the quantities involved – and the time it will take for the supplies to arrive in the US – is “too little, too late” to affect current high diesel prices, which observers have linked to challenging Republican party polling numbers before next month’s midterm elections.

US prices have surged by almost 70% since the start of the Iran war, to about $6.30 a gallon, according to American Automobile Association. In the UK, the average price of diesel climbed to a record £2 a litre earlier in October, and sat just below that mark on Friday.
Ashley Kelty, an energy analyst with the investment bank Panmure Liberum, said: “It is not going to have any impact on prices. The first amount [due to be shipped to the US] is so small.

“They are going to have to charter vessels, load them and transport the cargo to the US. That will take about three weeks – so we are pretty much at the end of the month and about a week before the midterms.”
The US Treasury secretary, Scott ⁠Bessent, said on Sunday: “This is ​good ‌for the ​American ​people … bringing these diesel prices down.”

However, Kelty said the diesel shipments would also cause complications in a global supply chain, including multinational companies having to work out which of its supplies originated from Russia and therefore might breach sanctions in other jurisdictions, including Europe.
The US Treasury suspended sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, while keeping in place other sanctions on Russian products.

Zelenskyy described Trump’s deal as a “weak decision”, saying it would encourage Russia to keep attacking Ukraine, but Trump then blamed Kyiv’s strikes on Russian energy infrastructure for rising fuel prices. Trump said Ukraine neeeded “a new leader”.
On Sunday, Zelenskyy said he would be ready to stop hitting Russian oil refineries if Russia curbed its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

Trump later posted on Truth Social: “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it! Thank you for your attention to this matter.”

Maximilian Hess, the founder of the political risk consultancy Enmetena Advisory and a fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute, said: “It will not have any meaningful domestic US effect or international effect given its full terms are highly unlikely to be met as a result of the impact of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refining which have limited its diesel output.
“The whole point of the deal for Putin is that it fails, which he can blame on Ukraine and thus stoke tensions between Trump and Zelenskyy. Indeed, it’s already working.”

articles.title: Poland stabbings driven by online glorification of violence, Tusk says
articles.summary: The PM was speaking after violent attacks at Polish schools this week left one dead and others injured.

blocks.text: Three violent attacks at Polish schools this week were driven by the "glorification of violence" online, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said.
The attacks have left one woman dead and others injured, including children.
"These are very often spontaneous actions inspired by online activity," Tusk said on Sunday, during a crisis meeting with security services.
Police have arrested 117 people across the country for possession knives or other weapons, or for threatening to attack schools or fellow students, after searching tens of thousands of schools.
A woman was arrested on Saturday after injuring three people while attacking a 17-year-old girl at an educational institution in the capital, Warsaw.
It came a day after thousands of police visited schools across Poland, following two stabbing attacks earlier in the week, one of which led to the killing of a female caretaker.
"We are not dealing with any group organized on a big scale," Tusk said on Sunday.
"In the past years and months, we have noted - globally and in Poland - a rise in the fascination with violence," he added.
The prime minister said the attacks were acts "nihilistic violence" associated with the extreme right.

"Some of the people detained are active in the ultraright environment," he said, adding that police had noticed a rise in online searches of Nazi content as well as of "mass killers who have become idols online".
On Wednesday, a 19-year-old student attacked and injured nine people at a vocational school in the central Polish province of Mazovian.
A day later, the 37-year-old caretaker was killed after a 15-year-old entered a primary school in Leszczydół-Nowiny, north of Warsaw.

Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński also said a 17-year-old was detained in the town of Sierpc, north-west of Warsaw, after allegedly stating "on school grounds that he planned to do something... dangerous - that he intended to harm someone".

Thousands of Polish ‌police officers visited schools nationwide to try to reassure pupils after the stabbings sparked rumours of a "Bloody Friday" of more attacks stemming from a supposed online challenge.

Meanwhile, Polish security services convened a special meeting on Sunday after receiving information about a potential attack on Tusk and Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, a spokesperson said.
A special services spokesman said officials were treating the threat as "deadly serious".

articles.title: Zelenskyy rejects Trump claim of Ukraine and Russia ‘energy ceasefire’ – live updates
articles.summary:
Ukraine’s president says Kyiv would accept a deal if Moscow does after US president posts announcement with no detail on social media

The latest acrimonious row between Washington and Kyiv…

blocks.text: Zelenskyy says ceasefire 'was news for me' but Kyiv would accept it if Moscow does
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskiy ⁠has said the “energy ceasefire” was news to him.

He told the news outlet ⁠Axios ​that he was not aware of ⁠an “energy ceasefire” between Ukraine and Russia announced by ​ ‌Donald Trump, but ‌added that if Moscow ‌agreed to such a ceasefire, Kyiv would accept it.

“The ceasefire announcement was news for ‌me. But if Russians agree to an energy ​ceasefire Ukraine will agree. If president Trump negotiated it with ⁠Putin — please tell us ​when ​the ceasefire begins — we ​are ready and ​we ‌will ​accept ​it,” Zelenskiy was quoted as saying by Axios.
Key events

37m agoTrump claims Russia and Ukraine agree to stop attacks on energy infrastructure

blocks.text: A senior Ukrainian official has also reportedly told the FT that Ukraine had no information about Trump’s proclaimed ceasefire deal.
The official was quoted as saying: “Just now our repair teams are restoring electricity and water supplies in Kyiv” following Russian strikes. “Nobody has heard [of the ceasefire].”
Donald Trump’s call for Zelenskyy to make way for a new Ukrainian leader drew criticism from his own party.
Don Bacon, a Republican Nebraska congressman and former military officer, suggested Trump was not fit to lead.
Reacting to Trump’s statement that “it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president’”, Bacon wrote on: “We need a president who is up to the task of leading the free world.”

blocks.caption: Luke Harding

blocks.text: Luke Harding

The latest acrimonious row between Washington and Kyiv began on Friday when Trump announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports. He said the move would reduce global and domestic fuel prices before next month’s US midterm elections.

A furious Zelenskyy called the decision “weak” and said it would generate “billions” in extra revenue for Putin, enabling him to wage war “even more intensely”. An equally irate Trump warned that Zelenskyy should “damn well stop” hitting Russian refineries. Ukraine needed a “new leader”, he said on Saturday.

Responding to Trump, Zelenskyy said it was up to Ukraine’s society to chose “one or another leader”. He told ABC News he was willing to bow down to US demands and to organise elections, but only if Putin agreed to a “total” sixty-day ceasefire.
In his Truth Social post, Trump gave no further details. The US president had made a similar claim in September, which turned out to be untrue.
Ukraine’s government did not immediately comment on the US president’s latest statement, or confirm a deal had taken place.
Just hours before Donald Trump claimed the two sides had agreed a ceasefire on energy strikes, Volodymyr Zelenskyy rebuffed his demand that Ukraine stop bombing Russian oil refineries.
Zelenskyy demanded Moscow has to first halt its own “brutal” attacks on Ukraine and its energy infrastructure.

Ukraine’s president said any deal to end his country’s long-range drone strikes on targets inside Russia would have to be “reciprocal”. It should be backed by “real guarantees” – meaning punitive measures against Moscow from Ukraine’s allies, including the US.
Trump claims Russia and Ukraine agree to stop attacks on energy infrastructure
Donald Trump has claimed Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an ”energy ceasefire”, though the US president gave no details of the purported agreement.
“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on his Truth Social network.

Trump made the announcement on his Truth Social account shortly after Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, told ABC on Sunday that Ukraine was ready for a ceasefire, including on energy infrastructure.
This announcement follows Trump’s criticism of Zelenskyy for attacks on Russian diesel facilities, which he blames for global shortages.
