articles.title: A migrant boat sank off the coast of Djibouti with the UN reporting over 200 people dead or missing
articles.summary: The UN migration agency has reported that at least 109 people were killed and 116 remain missing after a migrant boat sank overnight on its way to Yemen. At least 80 Ethiopians survived the incident…

image.caption: The UN migration agency IOM has called for donors to help Djibouti's rescue efforts, as Red Sea crossings — and sinkings — increase dramaticallyImage: Luis Tato/AFP

blocks.text: The United Nations International Organization for Migration (IOM) on Sunday said that 109 people were killed, 80 survived and 116 remained missing after the overnight sinking of a migrant boat off the coast of Djibouti in northeastern Africa.
The vessel, which was estimated to have been carrying 350 people, capsized near Obock, Djibouti, en route to Yemen.

In a statement, IOM Chief of Mission in Djibouti Alexandre Coissac called the loss of life "devastating," adding, "This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities" by trying to cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Yemen and reach Gulf countries.
"Poverty, insecurity and the growing impacts of climate change drive many to undertake this journey, despite mounting instability across the Middle East," according to the IOM.
IOM representatives said, "Djiboutian authorities are continuing search and rescue operations as fears grow for those still missing."
Djibouti to Yemen a dangerous crossing

The IOM says it has detected more than 20,000 crossings from Djibouti to Yemen — which is currently in the middle of a raging civil war — in the past month. More than 900 migrants were killed attempting the passage in 2025.
The IOM says most of those attempting to cross are from Ethiopia and Somalia. The 80 survivors from Saturday night's capsizing were all Ethiopian nationals.
The IMO on Sunday urged "donors and partners to strengthen support for Djibouti's response, including search and rescue operations and life-saving assistance."
Of the bodies so far recovered, 52 were men, 42 were women and 15 were children.
Bab el-Mandeb trade disruption: What it means for Djibouti

articles.title: Riyadh airport attack another dangerous moment in already tense conflict
articles.summary: The Houthis have stepped up their attacks on Saudi Arabian soil, and while the physical damage can be quickly repaired, its reputation for stability is taking a battering.

blocks.text: Not since the al-Qaeda insurgency of the mid-2000s has the Kingdom faced such a serious threat.

The Saudi government overcame that challenge through an effective hearts and minds campaign. Then it weathered the Arab Spring uprisings around the region which saw off leaders in Tunisia, Libya, Egypt and Yemen.
It even shrugged off – with some annoyance – an Iranian ballistic missile attack on Riyadh in March.

But this is different. Saudi Arabia may have one of the most powerful air forces in the Middle East, and it has been carrying out devastating air strikes on Houthi positions. Despite this, the opposing forces have managed to seize large portions of the war-torn country, particularly in the north and west.
But the Houthis know exactly where to hit back: at the soft underbelly of the Saudi economy.

As part of the "axis of resistance", the Houthis are a vital strategic partner for Iran. From Jizan on the Red Sea to the petrochemical complex at Khurais, the Houthis are delivering explosive drones and missiles with deadly accuracy.

The Red Sea shipping route has become increasingly important, because the Strait of Hormuz, on the other side of the Gulf, has still not fully reopened since the US and Iran have failed to reach a deal to end their war.
Targeting ships in the Red Sea is another way that the Houthis are trying to exert leverage - the attacks cause global economic damage, which is a key bargaining chip for Tehran.

In early September, the White House stated it would not directly intervene in the Yemen conflict, but could provide intelligence support to the Saudis. It later confirmed that it was supplying intelligence and had deployed military experts to Saudi Arabia.
However the situation may have taken a new turn following the latest attack on Riyadh, which killed a US citizen.
Speaking to reporters, US President Donald Trump called Saturday's attack "terrible" and indicated he may intervene militarily with the Saudis.
"We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision. We move very quickly," Trump said.
But that now seems unlikely, at least before crucial US midterm elections next month.

When he was re-elected in 2024, Trump promised to end America's role in wars around the world. Despite this, the US is currently involved in three unresolved conflicts in the Middle East - in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
Should Trump get embroiled in another one, this time in Yemen, it is unlikely to go down well with voters.
This war now looks like it will intensify before it ends in another shaky truce - with or without US involvement.
Additional analysis from Abdelbassir Hassan, BBC Arabic

articles.title: Pope Leo to have surgery after lump found on lung
articles.summary: The 71-year-old pontiff said the nodule was identified "at a very early stage".

blocks.text: Pope Leo XIV has announced he will be operated "in the coming days" after a nodule was found on his lung during a medical check up.
"The doctors found an early, well-localised nodule on my lung," he told the public during his weekly Sunday prayers in St Peter's Square in Rome.
The 71-year-old pontiff said his medical team "believe it would be right to intervene" and he had agreed to the operation.
Pope Leo reassured pilgrims that the mass was "well-contained" and caught "at an early stage".
He concluded his Angelus prayer by thanking everyone for their "spiritual closeness" and said he entrusted himself to their prayers.
Holy See Press Office spokesperson Matteo Bruni told the media that "the operation is scheduled for the first days of next week".
Bruni added that the Pope is expected to take about a week to recover.
Vatican News, the Holy See's news portal, said the operation will take place at Gemelli Hospital in Rome.
The hospital set up a special Papal suite following the failed assassination attempt on Pope John Paul II's life in May 1981, which is still in use today.
Pope Leo, born Robert Francis Provost, succeeded Pope Francis in 2025. He is the 267th occupant of the throne of St Peter – and is the first American.
He was ordained in 1982 and spent years as a missionary in Peru, where he is remembered as a figure who worked with marginalised communities and helped build bridges.

articles.title: Lino Cayetano to replace Dave Gomez as PCO chief
articles.summary: Former Taguig City Mayor Lino Cayetano is expected to replace Dave Gomez as head of the Presidential Communications Office (PCO), President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. announced on Sunday.

blocks.text: Published October 11, 2026 7:13pm
Former Taguig City Mayor Lino Cayetano is expected to replace Dave Gomez as head of the Presidential Communications Office (PCO), President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. announced on Sunday.
Marcos made the announcement during a media interview at the conclusion of his five-day working visit to Singapore on Sunday.
“Na-bypass si Dave, so I guess, immediately, at least, who will take his place is Lino,” Marcos said.
The President added that the change in leadership would be formalized upon their return to the Philippines.
“It's just a matter of formalizing everything,” he said.
Marcos' announcement came as he concluded his five-day working visit to Singapore on October 11, 2026.
Cayetano would be the sixth official to head the PCO under the Marcos administration, following Trixie Cruz-Angeles, Cheloy Velicaria-Garafil, Cesar Chavez, Jay Ruiz and Dave Gomez.

Gomez's bypassed appointment came amid tensions within the Senate and the Commission on Appointments in June, as political realignments following the Senate leadership change reshaped the commission's composition and voting dynamics.

Cayetano, a former congressman and television director, previously served as mayor of Taguig City from 2019 to 2022. He is a member of the Cayetano political family, which includes his siblings, senators Alan Peter and Pia Cayetano, who now belong to the minority bloc in the Senate.

In June 2026, Cayetano was appointed general manager of the government-run People's Television Network (PTV-4), an attached government-owned and controlled corporation (GOCC) of the PCO. He took his oath before Gomez, who was then PCO acting secretary.

Before entering government, Cayetano worked as a television director and creative consultant. He served as representative of Taguig-Pateros' second congressional district from 2013 to 2016 and as Taguig City mayor from 2019 to 2022.— With a report from Jonathan Andal/MCG, GMA News

articles.title: WPS fishers ask Sara Duterte if 'China money' bought her silence
articles.summary: Fisherfolk who depend on the West Philippine Sea for their livelihood have questioned whether reports of Vice President Sara Duterte"s alleged China-linked financial transactions explain her silence…

blocks.text: Published October 11, 2026 7:09pm

Fisherfolk who depend on the West Philippine Sea for their livelihood have questioned whether reports of Vice President Sara Duterte’s alleged China-linked financial transactions explain her silence on Beijing’s maritime aggression against Filipino fishers.

At a press conference organized by ATIN TO, fishers from Zambales and Bataan called for clear answers, particularly as Filipino fishers continue to face intimidation, dangerous encounters and restrictions in their traditional fishing grounds.

“Madam VP Sara, kaya po ba tahimik kayo sa gitna ng karahasan at kalupitan na sinasapit namin sa West Philippine Sea sa kamay ng Tsina ay dahil nabayaran ng milyones ang inyong katahimikan?” said Leonardo “Ka Nards” Cuaresma, president of the New Masinloc Fishermen Association.
(Madam VP Sara, are you silent amid the violence and cruelty we suffer in the West Philippine Sea at the hands of China because millions were paid for your silence?)

Cuaresma questioned the reported China-linked financial transactions involving Duterte and her husband, contrasting them with the harassment and intimidation Filipino fishers face from Chinese vessels in the West Philippine Sea.

“Habang kami ay hinaharass, tinatakot, pinagnanakawan ng huling isda at itinataboy ng mga barko ng China sa sarili naming karagatan, ang Bise Presidente at ang kanyang asawa ay diumano tumanggap ng milyon-milyon mula sa China," he said.
(While we are being harassed, intimidated, robbed of our catch and driven away by Chinese vessels in our own waters, the Vice President and her husband allegedly received millions from China.)
"Hindi ba isa itong katrayduran? Hindi ba dapat ipaliwanag ito sa taumbayan?” he added.
(Isn’t this an act of betrayal? Shouldn’t this be explained to the public?)

During Duterte’s impeachment trial, the Anti-Money Laundering Council confirmed that Cale88 Foods Corporation, a company linked to the Vice President and her husband, lawyer Mans Carpio, received about P319 million from China and Hong Kong.
The fisherfolk said every time Filipino fishing boats are driven away or their crews are intimidated, the fishers lose income and their families struggle to meet their basic needs.
Cuaresma urged Duterte and her husband to explain the nature, source and purpose of the reported China-linked financial transactions.

“For us, the impeachment trial of the Vice President is not only about unexplained and ill-gotten wealth. This is about our livelihood, our safety, and our country’s sovereignty. We face the risks at sea, and we deserve leaders who will stand up for us, not multimillionaire traitors,” Cuaresma said.
“Ang West Philippine Sea ay atin. Hindi dapat ang milyones ng Tsina ang manaig sa karapatan ng mga mangingisdang Pilipino na mangisda nang malaya at ligtas sa sarili nilang karagatan,” he added.
(The West Philippine Sea is ours. China’s millions should not prevail over the rights of Filipino fishers to fish freely and safely in their own waters.)

The fishers challenged Duterte to condemn China’s harassment of Filipino fishers in the West Philippine Sea and affirm that protecting national sovereignty takes precedence over her private interests.
GMA News has reached out to Duterte’s office for comment and will publish its response once available. —MCG, GMA News

articles.title: 'Disrespect for wildlife': Multiple grizzly bear poaching incidents under investigation in Alberta
articles.summary: Provincial officials are investigating the illegal killings of four grizzly bears at three separate locations over the last year. One of the bear corpses was found abandoned with its paws removed…

image.caption: A file photo of a grizzly bear in Kananaskis Country. The illegal killings of four grizzlies at three separate locations in Alberta this year are under investigation. One of the bears was found abandoned with its paws removed after being poached. (Amir Said/CBC)

blocks.text: Calgary

Provincial officials are investigating the illegal killings of four grizzly bears at three separate locations over the last year. One of the bear corpses was found abandoned with its paws removed after being poached.
Body of bear found abandoned with paws removed in northern Alberta
WARNING: This story contains graphic images of grizzly bears killed by poachers.
Provincial officials are investigating multiple cases of poachers killing grizzly bears in Alberta.
The province told CBC News that Alberta Fish and Wildlife Enforcement Services is investigating the illegal killings of four grizzly bears at three separate locations.
One grizzly bear was found shot dead Sept. 30, along a road about 20 kilometres north of Swan Hills, northwest of Edmonton.
The next day on Oct. 1, another grizzly was found dead in a remote area between Little Smoky and Fox Creek. All four of the bear's paws had been removed.
It comes after two grizzly bears were found shot dead in June along a road near Sundre, about 95 kilometres northwest of Calgary.
And in March of this year, the province announced it was seeking public assistance in a poaching investigation after a grizzly bear was found dead from a gunshot wound in November 2025.
"The illegal killing of any grizzly bear is taken seriously," the province told CBC News in a statement.

This grizzly bear was found dead off Deep Valley Road between Little Smoky and Fox Creek in northern Alberta on Oct. 1. The bear had been shot and moved off the main trail, and all four of its paws had been removed. (Alberta Fish and Wildlife Enforcement/Facebook)
Hunting grizzlies has been banned in Alberta since 2006, with the exception of harvesting by Indigenous hunters for subsistence or cultural purposes.

The province is asking that anyone with information about these poaching incidents or other suspected wildlife offences contact the Report-A-Poacher line or submit a report online at alberta.ca/report-poacher.
Through the province's Report-A-Poacher program, a tipster who provides information leading to charges being laid could be eligible for a cash reward.
'Disregard and disrespect for wildlife'

Gordon Stenhouse, the biologist behind much of Alberta's grizzly bear population research, said shooting grizzly bears and abandoning their bodies is "disappointing" but doesn't surprise him, as "people have been doing that for a long time."
"To shoot and leave any animal, and especially a grizzly bear, a threatened species, shows a disregard and disrespect for wildlife," he said.
This grizzly bear was found shot dead on Sept. 30, about 20 kilometres north of Swan Hills in northern Alberta. (Alberta Fish and Wildlife Enforcement/Facebook)
Stenhouse said it's likely the number of bears found after being poached is "probably only a fraction of what's actually happening."
"I think there's lots of bears that are never found," he said.

items: More grizzly bears killed in 2024 than any other year on record in Alberta
Grizzly bear killings have spiked through provincial program; government says recovery still priority

blocks.text: The Alberta government keeps track of human-caused grizzly bear mortality. From 2020 to 2025, there were 28 documented cases of grizzly bears killed illegally — about 17 per cent of grizzly bear deaths during that time. Other leading causes of grizzly bear mortality include being killed by the province and struck by vehicles.
Grizzly bears have been a threatened species in Alberta since 2010.

University of Alberta ecology professor Mark Boyce said he doesn't consider poaching "a major issue" when it comes to grizzly bear conservation, but he considers these latest incidents "really unfortunate."
"There's a black market for grizzly bear paws," he said. "It's highly illegal, but poaching the bear was highly illegal in the first place."
A file photo of Mark Boyce, ecology professor and Alberta Conservation Association chair in fisheries and wildlife at the University of Alberta. (BoompaCanada/Flickr)
In addition to financial motivation, Boyce said poaching can happen because people hate or fear grizzly bears.
Better co-existence needed: bear safety expert
Bear Safety and More founder Kim Titchener says she considers poaching a symptom of a larger conflict between humans and bears struggling to share the landscape.
"We do live with grizzly bears in Alberta," Titchener said. "When they come into communities, walk onto a golf course, go onto a rancher's land ... we start to see conflicts with these animals."
"For some people, it creates a lot of fear and they want to get rid of bears. For other people, they want to try to live with these animals."

items: Grizzly bear trapped, killed after trying to break into central Alberta chicken coop
Honey-hunting grizzlies are 'one of the realities' for beekeepers in Bearberry, Alta.

blocks.text: Titchener says communities in and around bear country should prioritize resources such as electric fencing, guard dogs and bear-resistant containers over killing grizzly bears.

"You can go and shoot and kill that bear that is killing your chickens, but another bear is just going to show up and eat your chickens too," she said. "So you really need to address the cause of this."

items: Conservation groups call for 'science-based' approach to Alberta grizzly bear hunt proposal
'No plans right now' for grizzly hunting season in Alberta, minister says as rural residents call for hunt

blocks.text: The Alberta government announced in 2024 it would invest $700,000 over five years to help keep large carnivores away from rural properties in southwestern Alberta, including setting up electric fencing, upgrading grain bins and removing dead livestock.
The province supports BearSmart programs across Alberta in an effort to minimize the risk of human-wildlife conflict and reduce grizzly bear deaths.
The province estimates there are about 1,000 grizzlies in Alberta today, though there hasn't been a provincial grizzly bear population study since 2018.

Amir Said is a multimedia journalist with CBC Calgary. He is an alumnus of the University of Regina, and his award-winning work as a writer and photographer has been published by outlets across Canada, including Postmedia, The Hill Times and The Narwhal. articles.title: Disappointed, angry, excited: Albertans weigh in on looming referendum
articles.summary: At a library branch CBC News visited in Calgary, a few people were excited to vote. Others were just starting to follow the process, and several expressed frustration at Alberta even having a…

image.caption: CBC Radio's The Homestretch host Jenny Howe interviewed Calgarian Jim Fedor at the Calgary Public Library’s Seton branch on Thursday. He shared his plans to vote on Oct. 19. (Elise Stolte/CBC)

blocks.text: Calgary

At a library branch CBC News visited in Calgary, a few people were excited to vote. Others were just starting to follow the process, and several expressed frustration at Alberta even having a referendum.
CBC News heard a lot about unity and unease at a pop-up in a Calgary library
Jim Fedor booked Oct. 19 off work to make sure he can vote in Alberta’s referendum.

“I'm looking forward to it. Never voted in a referendum like this before, so it'll be something new,” said Fedor, who stopped at the CBC News pop-up at the Seton library branch in southeast Calgary last week.

“I'm gonna vote Option 1 on the separation question, for Alberta to stay in Canada, and the other nine questions I plan to vote no for each one,” he said. “I'll get there early, and I'm willing to wait to get in and vote.”
“I think it's important for everyone to have their voices heard. A lot of places in the world don't allow voting on much of anything. So I feel quite lucky to be able to vote and make my vote count.”

items: Follow all of our Alberta referendum coverage

blocks.text: CBC News set up at the library to get a sense of how Albertans are feeling as the referendum campaigns head into their final week. We set out Post-It notes and markers, and invited patrons to share their thoughts on the question: What are you thinking about as you get ready to vote?
Library patrons left their thoughts at a CBC News pop-up in the Calgary Public Library's Seton branch. (Elise Stolte/CBC)
Parents came by with their kids; high school students stopped in after their classes ended; seniors swung by to pick up books on hold. A low hum filled the busy building.
Some Albertans frustrated at the vote

A few people were excited to vote, like Fedor. Others were just starting to follow the process and had not yet decided how they would cast their ballots; several expressed frustration at even having the vote.

items: 'People are overwhelmed': Community groups rally to inform voters ahead of Alberta referendum
Albertans divided on immigration, while half still undecided on 9 non-separation questions: poll

blocks.text: That’s how Christine Nelson was feeling.

“I'm really disappointed. The majority of people do not want to separate, and we have to spend taxpayers’ money to vote on something that's not going to go through unless there's some kind of, you know, crookedness going on. It's ridiculous,” said Nelson.
Charmaine Coutinho, who stopped by with her young daughter, had a similar sentiment.

“I am feeling anger about the increase in racism and otherness caused by legitimizing these extreme perspectives through government actions,” she said. “I am saying no to everything, and we are, and I am, very much in favour of staying in Canada.”

From left to right, Michael Chudleigh, Charmaine Coutinho and her daughter, and Christine Nelson. They all stopped by to share their thoughts at the CBC News pop-up in Seton on Thursday. (Elise Stolte/CBC)
Michael Chudleigh said he is voting the same, but trying to stay open to difference.
“I'm trying not to be angry about the whole thing and understand that those who disagree with me have their reasons, even if I can't see them.”
Friends at odds over separation
One pair of seniors were laughing and chatting as they stopped by on their way for coffee. The two women said they are good friends, who meet regularly.
One is passionate about staying in Canada, while the other is casting her vote to explore leaving.

They don’t talk about the referendum. “We might not be friends after!” said the pro-unity friend. She didn’t want to be interviewed, but earlier said her father fought for Canada and she’d never want to see it splintered.

The other friend came back later to write her thoughts on the whiteboard: “I think the Oct. 19 [referendum] is more like a memorandum of understanding thing and gets people talking and looking into our rights and fairness/democracy. But many people have been led to be afraid it’s a final say or referendum to leave their country or be taken over by Trump!”
She wrote that separatists fear the way Ottawa has been asserting control over individuals, such as freezing bank accounts during the trucker convoy.

items: First came the blockade. Then came separatism. Old tensions revived in Coutts
How anti-COVID activism injected life into Alberta's separatist movement

blocks.text: Newcomers express love for Canada
As the afternoon wore on, our board filled with messages, with a lot of love for Canada.
“I love Canada; I’ll vote to stay here,” wrote one person.
“I love Canada, this is my home,” wrote another.

David Aldana immigrated from Colombia and has been following the referendum campaigns, even though he can't vote. Other Albertans with permanent residency but no Canadian citizenship also left messages on the board. (Elise Stolte/CBC)
Several people with permanent residency but not Canadian citizenship stopped by. One was David Aldana, who moved to Canada from Colombia.

“If I could vote, I would stay with Canada, and because I feel that unity is better,” he said. “I think unity is better for the country itself. I'm in love with Canada. I'm in love with the freedom that we have here.”
Concerns the vote could backfire
In Alberta, support for independence had been polling at about 27 per cent this spring, according to a poll from Janet Brown Opinion Research commissioned by CBC News.

That softened to 23 per cent in a similar poll by Janet Brown in September, which also found Premier Danielle Smith’s United Conservative Party lost some support, likely due to frustration over the vote.

One man at the library called it a nightmare. He wrote: “Talk about backfiring. Rather than more consideration from Ottawa we are now facing a potential NDP resurgence (the worst outcome you could imagine).”

On the left, a Ukrainian newcomer left her concerns: the referendum reminds her of separation votes in the Ukrainian regions of Crimea and Donbas. On the right, a public servant wrote a note about his hope for a transparent referendum process. (Elise Stolte/CBC)
Muaaz Asher is a Grade 10 student who stopped by after class at the nearby Joane Cardinal-Schubert High School. He said at school they tried to look at the separation arguments from both sides.

“Surprisingly, a lot of my class wanted to stay. And I really found that fascinating ‘cause there's just one of my friends who is heavily right. He always agrees with whatever right-wingers say but this time … he wants to stay in Canada,” Asher said.
“It kind of just shows that as a country — it sounds a bit corny, but there's a lot of love and unity. I think that's really special, and I think we just can't give that up.”
Muaaz Asher is a Grade 10 student who discussed the Alberta referendum question at school. (Elise Stolte/CBC)
'Strong opinions on both sides'
The voices for unity were loudest and most common at the library Thursday. But it’s one location, on one afternoon.

items: Poll suggests slight majority of UCP voters favours separation as party stares down ‘tough days’ ahead
Fight for independence won't end after referendum: Alberta Prosperity Project leader

blocks.text: Destiny Fox stopped by and suggested you can’t judge how people in general are feeling by those most willing to speak up.

“I don't think that a lot of people are being very open about their opinion to leave Canada as honestly as people who want to stay in Canada,” Fox said. “So you're just not hearing as much … You're not going to see the lawn signs on people's personal property because they don't want to get into it with their neighbours. But I think that there are a lot of strong opinions on both sides.

“I'm glad that we're having this referendum because I feel like it's giving everybody an opportunity to voice their feelings. And I don't necessarily feel that I want to separate from Canada, but I do want the premier to have the power to go back to Ottawa and say this is how Albertans are feeling.”
Turning Alberta referendum polling data into art
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Elise Stolte runs project-based engagement efforts for the CBC Calgary newsroom. She has 20 years of experience telling the stories of her community and has been recognized for feature writing, social impact and community-based journalism. You can reach her at elise.stolte@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Poland arrests man over plot to kill PM Donald Tusk
articles.summary: Prime Minister Donald Tusk confirmed the arrest hours after police received information about a possible assassination plot. Poland is still reeling from a wave of school violence this week.

image.caption: Amid a spate of violence this week, Tusk said 'spontaneous' attacks were 'inspired by online activity' [FILE: October 8]Image: Albert Zawada/PAP/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Poland on Sunday detained a man accused of plotting to assassinate Prime Minister Donald Tusk and the country's defense minister, the PM wrote on X.
"The man threatening an attack has been detained," Tusk wrote on X, praising the police for their "swift and decisive action."
The Interior Minister also confirmed the arrest. No details about the man's identity were made public.
Security chiefs convene urgent talks

Tusk's tweet followed an emergency meeting by Poland's security services to discuss what officials said was a potential attack against both the prime minister and Defense ‌Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz.
The meeting was convened at short notice after police received a tip-off about a possible assassination attempt, a spokesperson for the Interior Ministry wrote in a post on X.
While the nature of the apparent threat was not immediately clear, Poland remains on high alert after a wave of violent attacks at schools in the country this week.
Poland, which borders Ukraine, has also been facing growing security threats from hybrid attacks by Russia in recent months.
What do we know about the school attacks in Poland?
Poland is reeling from three knife attacks at schools in just four days this week, which have left at least one person dead and injured many others, including children.

The first incident was on Wednesday, when a 19-year-old student at a vocational school in the central Mazovian province injured nine people when he attacked his fellow students and teachers with a sharp object.

A day later, a 15-year-old killed a school caretaker and injured two others at his former school in Leszczydol-Nowiny, also in the same province. Tusk said the suspect had worn a camera mounted to his helmet to film the attack.
On Saturday, a 21-year-old woman attacked an adult education school in Warsaw, wounding three other women.

Polish police have detained 117 people across the country for carrying knives or dangerous weapons, as well as for threatening to attack schools or students. Police checked 64,000 schools, most of them in central Mazovian province.
Police said Friday that cybercrime investigators have found no evidence that a social media challenge is fueling the wave of youth violence, or that the attacks were coordinated.
What did Tusk say about the school attacks?
On Sunday morning, Donald Tusk said the attacks were "spontaneous actions" that were fueled by rising "glorification of violence" online.
"We are not dealing with any group organized on a big scale," Tusk said during the government crisis meeting.
"In the past years and months, we have noted — globally and in Poland — a rise in the fascination with violence," Tusk continued.

The prime minister blamed "nihilistic violence" for the wave of attacks, rather than a specific political ideology. However, he did acknowledge that "some of the people detained are active in the ultraright environment."
Tusk added that authorities have observed an increase in online searches for Nazi or far-right content and for "mass killers who have become idols online."
The prime minister pointed to a "civilizational phenomenon" of children becoming more exposed to violence online through video games or crime stories.

Tusk added that police checks would continue at schools across the country next week to make sure children who have been exposed to these stories of knife attacks do not "get stupid and unsafe thoughts" of perpetrating copycat attacks.

It is believed that the flood was caused by a landslide upstream of the Budhi Gandaki River in the Gorkha district.
Four bridges and nearly two dozen houses have been swept away, as well as a camp at a hydropower project along the river.

Nepal is still trying to recover from catastrophic floods and landslides that swept through its border towns with Tibet two months ago, wiping out thousands of houses, destroying critical energy infrastructure and leaving thousands dead and missing.

articles.title: Marcos: Sara Duterte's alleged China funds pose 'highest-level' national security threat
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said the alleged receipt of funds from China by a company linked to Vice President Sara Duterte could pose a national security threat “at the highest level” if proven…

blocks.text: Published October 11, 2026 6:01pm

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said the alleged receipt of funds from China by a company linked to Vice President Sara Duterte could pose a national security threat “at the highest level” if proven true.
During Duterte’s impeachment trial, the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) confirmed that a company linked to the Vice President and her husband received P319 million from China and Hong Kong.
“The most disturbing aspect of it is the Chinese money that now rises to a national security issue, kung totoo (if it is true). If it is true, it is a national security issue,” Marcos said.
The alleged financial transactions were raised during the impeachment court proceedings on Article II of the complaint, which accuses Duterte of amassing unexplained wealth, among other allegations.
Marcos said he hoped the allegations against the Vice President would be disproven.

“Nothing would make me happier than proof that it is not true. Then it's one less thing that I have to worry about. But if it is true, it is a threat at the highest level to the Republic,” Marcos said.
The President also cited investigations initiated by the Department of National Defense into the allegations, underscoring the potential national security implications of the reported transactions.
On Tuesday, the National Security Council (NSC) said it was taking the allegations seriously and would look into reported financial inflows from China to a company linked to Duterte’s family.

“The NSC will look into the information presented and, as a matter of policy, continue to task the intelligence and investigative agencies and coordinate with relevant government institutions to assess the national security implications, if any, arising from the reported transactions,” National Security Adviser Eduardo Oban Jr. said.
On Monday, Duterte's spokesperson, lawyer Salvador Paolo Panelo, said accusations that the Vice President has links to China because she allegedly received funds from the Chinese are without basis.

"There was a donation from the Chinese government to Tapang at Malasakit Foundation, and the Vice President is one of the trustees. Does that automatically mean the Chinese government is supporting the Vice President?" he said in Filipino.
“What if it was used to build classrooms? Or what if it was used for charitable purposes and there is proof?” Panelo added.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: [Inside the Newsroom] How Rappler uncovered Sara Duterte’s company contracts with Davao City Hall
articles.summary: Rappler has exposed government officials' conflicts of interest involving infrastructure projects. The story of Sara Duterte and Gencorp revealed that this kind of scheme can also happen in food…

blocks.text: Rappler has exposed government officials' conflicts of interest involving infrastructure projects. The story of Sara Duterte and Gencorp revealed that this kind of scheme can also happen in food contracts. And perhaps there are similar stories hiding in procurement records across the country.

items: Patrick Cruz, a public finance reporter for Rappler, shifted his focus to cover the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, specifically reporting on the senator-judges and related proceedings.

During his investigation, Cruz uncovered connections between Duterte and Gencorp, a company that won significant government contracts, raising questions about Duterte's financial disclosures and potential conflicts of interest.

Cruz emphasizes the importance of curiosity and thorough investigation in journalism, advocating for reporters to dig deeper into records and documents to uncover stories that may reveal corruption or conflicts of interest in government contracts.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Hello, I’m Patrick Cruz, Rappler’s public finance reporter.
My job is to follow the money — the people’s money — and track how it is allocated, spent, and misused.

My coverage, however, somehow shifted when I was tapped as one of three Rappler reporters assigned to cover the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte. I was assigned to cover the senator-judges, which meant reporting on the proceedings, the atmosphere inside the courtroom, and the decisions of the senator-judges.
One of the stories I wrote on July 20, 2026, involved the impeachment court’s issuance of subpoenas for the bank and tax records of companies linked to Duterte and her husband, Mans Carpio.

blocks.caption: REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK. Rappler multimedia reporter James Patrick Cruz takes notes on the third day of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on July 8, 2026.

blocks.text: That got me thinking: Are these companies also doing business with the government?

(After all, our country is run by politicians whose companies or their relatives’ companies earn billions of pesos out of infrastructure projects funded by hard earned money of Filipinos. We mapped them out here.)
I checked the companies linked to the Vice President one by one against government procurement records.
There, I found that Gencorp had won millions of pesos worth of food contracts from Davao City Hall and the PhilHealth Davao Regional Office.
That was the beginning of my two-month investigation.

I compiled the contracts into a Google Sheet and verified them one by one. I reviewed Duterte’s Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN) across several years and went through bidding documents, purchase orders, notices of award, and other procurement records.
We also bought Gencorp’s General Information Sheet filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). (Yes, we have to pay for these types of documents for our stories.)
But, instead of giving me more clarity, it brought me to another question: Why doesn’t Duterte’s name appear in the SEC records?
And then I also found something interesting: that businessman Jaime Tan Cruz is a shareholder of Gencorp.

Cruz is no stranger to former president Rodrigo Duterte, Sara’s father. The Duterte patriarch appointed him as Special Envoy to the People’s Republic of China for Trade and Investment. He was also considered for the post of PhilHealth president and CEO.

blocks.caption: INVESTIGATIVE BOARD. The chart shows the connections between the shareholders of Gencorp Industries Inc. and the Dutertes.

blocks.text: It later turned out that Cruz is a business partner of the Duterte siblings: Vice President Sara Duterte, Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte, and Davao City 1st District Representative Paolo “Pulong” Duterte.
The headline of our report, however, was criticized as “misleading” by Duterte’s spokesperson, Paolo Panelo. He argued that Gencorp was not the Vice President’s company.

So why did Duterte declare Gencorp as among her businesses in her SALN? Well, the Vice President has yet to answer this question. The fact remains that Gencorp is in the sworn SALN of the Vice President.
After our investigative report was published, the issue was tackled in the impeachment court in relation to Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth.

Davao City Mayor Baste Duterte, who was initially not listed as a witness in the trial, was compelled to appear before the court and answer questions about government contracts won by a company linked to his sister.

Before the court, Mayor Duterte said he did not know that his sister had an interest in Gencorp or that the company had won millions of pesos worth of contracts from the city government he is running.
In fact, he said the company had received even more contracts than those identified in our initial report.
At Rappler, our managers and editors often remind us to “move the story forward.”
For me, that starts with curiosity.

I could have stopped after reporting on the impeachment court’s subpoena for the records of Duterte-linked companies and called it a day. Instead, I dug into government procurement records to see what else the paper trail might reveal.

That, to me, is what it means to move a story forward. It means not stopping at the obvious news peg or covering a press conference, but digging through documents, checking records, following names, and pursuing the next lead.
Sometimes, that trail leads somewhere you did not expect.
That discipline has helped Rappler reporters produce investigative stories exposing conflicts of interest involving infrastructure projects in the wake of the flood control corruption scandal.
The story of Sara Duterte and Gencorp revealed that this kind of scheme can also happen in food contracts.
And perhaps there are similar stories hiding in procurement records across the country.

Maybe your local officials or their relatives have business interests that intersect with government contracts. Maybe they own a Jollibee or McDonald’s in your city and their business also supplies food for government events. Maybe they are suppliers of sound systems, laptops, or security services. Maybe they own a gas station where government vehicles buy their fuel.
If you know of a similar scheme, please report it to us at investigative@rappler.com.
You can also support more in-depth stories by donating to our investigative fund or joining the Rappler+ membership program. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Pakistan: President puts Khan stronghold province under emergency rule
articles.summary: President Asif Ali Zardari has effectively suspended the provincial government in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The northwestern state is an epicenter of support for former PM Imran Khan and run by his party.

image.caption: Authorities have set up massive roadblocks across Pakistan to keep Khan supporters at bayImage: Abdul Majeed/AFP

blocks.text: Pakistan's President Asif Ali Zardari on Sunday announced that the northwestern Pakistani province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa had been put under emergency rule, effectively removing power from former Prime Minster Imran Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party.
The imposition of emergency rule comes as thousands of Khan supporters continue to stage anti-government protests and demand the former leader be released from jail.
Current Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif proposed the move, which Zardari signed into order on Sunday.
The suspension of regional government was justified under constitutional articles that allow the central government to confront security threats and give it sweeping powers in emergency situations.
Sharif's government claims regional authorities have not done enough to curb Islamist violence in the province.
Why is Pakistan's government taking control of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa?

Last Sunday, thousands of Imran Khan supporters began to make their way from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to the Pakistani capital Islamabad, with organizers declaring their intent to rally hundreds of thousands more along the way in hopes of bringing about Khan's release from prison.

Despite being jailed since 2023, Khan, a popular former cricket star, maintains great influence in Pakistan, with he and his followers convinced that his imprisonment is the result of political persecution.
Khan, who began his term as prime minister in August 2018, left office in April 2022, when he lost a no-confidence vote.
He has been in prison since August 2023.
Beyond corruption and treason charges, he was also accused of inciting violence after widespread anti-government protests in May 2023.
Khan's supporters claim that the 2024 election that brought Shehbaz Sharif back to power was rigged — an accusation the government denies.

Pakistan has seen a resurgence of terror attacks over the past several months and the Sharif government accuses Khan's PTI of sympathizing with the Pakistani Taliban, also known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, which is largely thought to be behind the attacks.
The PTI rejects these accusations as a baseless smear campaign.

articles.title: Prosecution drops bribery charge 'to meet timetable'
articles.summary: The House prosecution panel in Vice President Sara Duterte"s impeachment trial has dropped the bribery charge against her to meet its timetable for presenting evidence, panel member and Bukidnon Rep.…

blocks.text: Published October 11, 2026 5:22pm

The House prosecution panel in Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial has dropped the bribery charge against her to meet its timetable for presenting evidence, panel member and Bukidnon Rep. Jonathan Keith Flores said Sunday.

“The only reason is the timetable. That’s really what we’re looking at. We want to finish this week because we’re about to go on a one-month break. We want the defense to begin after the break so the proceedings can continue smoothly,” Flores told Super Radyo dzBB.

Earlier this week, Flores announced that the prosecution had decided to drop Article III of the Articles of Impeachment, which contains the bribery allegations against Duterte, and informed the Senate Impeachment Court that it would conclude its presentation of evidence with Article II.

Flores told dzBB that the prosecution’s final witness would be lawyer Alexander Cabrera, a financial forensic analyst expected to tie together the tax and financial records of Duterte and her husband, lawyer Manases Carpio.
“So far, we believe the other articles have been sufficiently established and can stand on their own without the bribery article having to be tried before the impeachment court,” Flores said.
Flores added that the prosecution was preparing for the defense’s presentation of evidence.
The Senate Impeachment Court is currently hearing Article II of the Articles of Impeachment, which concerns Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth.
Article III, meanwhile, accuses the vice president of bribing officials of the Department of Education (DepEd) during her tenure as education secretary from 2022 to 2024.
The prosecution had earlier raised the possibility of referring the bribery allegations to the Department of Justice (DOJ) and the Office of the Ombudsman for possible criminal proceedings.

“Kung kailangan, we will be making the necessary endorsement so that the Ombudsman or the DOJ can conduct the preliminary investigation for the possible filing of the case of bribery against respondent [Duterte] and officials [of] DepEd [Department of Education],” House lead prosecutor Rep. Gerville Luistro said during a news forum in Quezon City.— Mariel Celine Serquiña/MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Panama declares state of emergency as powerful quake aftershocks rattle communities
articles.summary: The government of Panama declared a state of emergency Saturday as the aftershocks of two powerful earthquakes that roiled the country shook communities for hours. Officials did not attribute any…

image.caption: A car is covered in rubble from houses damaged by an earthquake in Villa de los Santos, Panama, Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. (Aris Mariota/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

The government of Panama declared a state of emergency Saturday as the aftershocks of two powerful earthquakes that roiled the country shook communities for hours. Officials did not attribute any deaths to the quakes but reported damages in all 10 of Panama's provinces and two Indigenous territories.
Most of the damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera, Cocle and Los Santos

The 7.7- and 6.6-magnitude earthquakes on Friday toppled buildings near the epicentre and prompted evacuations across the Central American country. Seismologists recorded more than 100 aftershocks, including ones measuring magnitude 5.8, 5.5 and 5.2.

The earlier quake, also felt in neighbouring Colombia, was centered about 10 kilometres southwest of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, in the central province of Herrera, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. It struck at a depth of 10 kilometres.

items: Powerful 7.7 magnitude earthquake rocks Panama

blocks.text: Presidential Minister Juan Carlos Orillac announced the emergency during a news conference in the capital, Panama City. He said homes, schools, healthcare facilities, roads and hotels were among the damaged facilities.
Malitzie Rivera, deputy director of the National Civil Protection System, told reporters the state had reports of 27 people with injuries, ranging from minor to moderate.
Hundreds of homes were damaged
Most of the damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera, Cocle and Los Santos.

The Civil Protection agency tallied roughly 420 homes and about the same number of public schools damaged. It also reported that seven hotels, at least 13 churches and nine bridges were affected by the earthquakes.

In La Villa de Los Santos, a colonial-era community about 64 kilometres northeast of the epicenter, homes and a historical Catholic church collapsed. People who spent the night on the streets were waiting for the government's guidance on what to do next.
Canadian in Panama experiences aftershock live on air | Hanomansing Live

"We've been here since 1 p.m. yesterday; we haven't moved," Tony Jimenez, whose home partially collapsed, said while sitting with relatives under a tent. "It was a terrible thing. I can tell you with absolute certainty that in my 90 years, I had never experienced anything like it. It was intense -- truly intense."
The collapsed Church of San Atanasio was declared a National Historic Heritage Site in 1938.
Images of crumbling buildings and deep fissures slicing through roads added to fears across a Latin American region battered by a series of devastating earthquakes in recent months.

Two back-to-back 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude earthquakes roiled Venezuela's La Guaira state in June, killing more than 6,500 people and leaving 17,000 homeless. In August, a 7.4 magnitude earthquake in Colombia killed at least 289 people.

The notably lower toll in nearby Panama may have been due to the country's strict building codes, especially governing construction of skyscrapers in the capital, said Carlos Valdes, head of the Seismology Department at the National Autonomous University of Mexico.
Rising sea levels prompt evacuations
Officials did not report any missing people on Saturday but said some communities remained cut off due to landslides and road damage.

On Isla Cana, off the Pacific coast of Los Santos, approximately 300 people were evacuated because of rising sea levels and rough surf. Meanwhile, in the city of Penonome, around 150 kilometres from the capital, a shelter was housing 13 people, including five children. The earthquakes caused a partial collapse and cracks at the cathedral in the district's main square, as well as damage to the governor's office building and the Dos Continentes hotel.
In Panama City, one of the water treatment plants supplying the area operated at 20 per cent capacity on Saturday, and tent facilities with cots were set up at six hospitals.

Tocumen International Airport in Panama City, one of the region's busiest airports with more than 20 million passengers in 2025, temporarily suspended operations after the first quake but said Friday but reopened hours later.
Powerful earthquake hits Panama, triggers tsunami warnings

But hundreds of travelers on major Panama-based airlines like Copa Airlines were left stranded in airports around the region. Their connections through Tocumen — one of the biggest travel hubs in the region — were canceled or delayed. In Mexico City's airport, airline employees scrambled as families with babies were sleeping on the floor Saturday while one woman from Venezuela shouted in panic that the flight through Panama was one of the only ways she could return home to Caracas.

The Panama Canal Authority said operations were continuing normally along the global trade route. It said its priority was the safety of employees, vessels and crews and that specialized technical teams were inspecting facilities for possible damage.

The last major earthquake to cause widespread damage in Panama struck in 1991. A magnitude 7.4 quake, centered in nearby Costa Rica, killed 23 people, injured 559 and left thousands of people homeless in the border Bocas del Toro region.
A vehicle lies crushed beneath a collapsed building after an earthquake struck Penonome, Panama, Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. (Aris Mariota/The Associated Press)
Earthquakes are common, especially along Panama's border with Costa Rica and its Pacific coast, because of the interaction of several tectonic plates, including the Cocos, Nazca and Caribbean plates.
Panama lies along the "Ring of Fire," a 40,000-kilometre arc of volcanoes and fault lines around the Pacific Basin, where most of the world's earthquakes occur.
Countries offer help

Messages of support and offers of assistance flooded in from across the region shortly after the earthquakes. Mulino on Friday thanked fellow Latin American leaders for their support, saying he had spoken with the presidents of Chile, Uruguay and Guatemala, among others.
The U.S. Department of State on Saturday said it mobilized a disaster response team to help local authorities with search and rescue expertise as well as aerial and on-the-ground assessments.
The U.S. government also pledged $5 million for humanitarian assistance.
U.S. Southern Command also said two helicopters supported by the State Department's drug-control bureau had delivered 2,000 pounds of food to Panamanian communities affected by the earthquakes.

articles.title: Germany rejects Trump demand, 'fully supports' Zelenskyy
articles.summary: Germany's foreign minister has said Berlin is behind Ukraine's president and will keep pressuring Russia to end its war. Meanwhile, Deutsche Bank's CEO warned that political extremism is spooking…

image.caption: Germany is Europe's largest Ukraine donor and Berlin says it continues to 'fully support' President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as his country defends itself against RussiaImage: Press Service of The President of Ukraine/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: October 11, 2026
Deutsche Bank CEO: Political extremism putting off foreign investors
Christian Sewing, CEO of Deutsche Bank, Germany's biggest, warned that the growing strength of both the far right and the far left is spooking foreign investors.

Sewing told the tabloid Bild that recent election victories for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and post-communist Left Party "pose a significant risk for Germany and should not be downplayed."

The Deutsche Bank boss said it mattered little that the elections were on the state and local level. "You can't expect a foreign investor to immediately draw a distinction ‌between a state government and Germany as a whole," he ‌said.
"It's ​seen as Germany as a whole and I think that from an investor's point of view, that's understandable."
Some economists say the AfD is creating an atmosphere that will drive away much needed skilled labor as well as foreign investors.
The Left Party, meanwhile, won victory in Berlin promising to expropriate residential property companies' holdings to lower housing costs in the German capital.
"Whether ​it's Saxony-Anhalt with ⁠the AfD or what's happening here in Berlin," said Sewing, "it's anything but conducive to economic growth. ⁠And it's anything ​but investment-friendly."

Sewing said Chancellor Friedrich Merz must get on with carrying out reforms and reviving the economy, saying, "That is the only response we have to the far-right and far-left extremists in this country."

articles.title: After 20 years as a P.E.I. firefighter, something snapped. Now he's teaching others about PTSD
articles.summary: Ernie Gallant was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder after dedicating two decades of volunteer service to the New Glasgow Fire Department in Prince Edward Island.

image.caption: Ernie Gallant, second from right, is pictured with members of the O'Leary Fire Department. Last year, Gallant started giving presentations to P.E.I. fire crews about his experience with post-traumatic stress disorder. (submitted by Ernie Gallant)

blocks.text: PEI
Ernie Gallant was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder after dedicating two decades of volunteer service to the New Glasgow Fire Department in Prince Edward Island.
Ernie Gallant says older firefighters can benefit most from speaking about trauma
In the summer of 2020, Ernie Gallant hit a wall. After 20 years as a volunteer firefighter, he says his body — and his mind — crashed.
"I didn’t know what was going on," he told Island Morning host Wayne Thibodeau. "My legs came out from under me and I was crying."
Gallant was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). He said those two decades of fighting fires in New Glasgow, P.E.I., likely played a major part in the development of the condition.
"Every time I come out of the driveway and looked left, I was triggered," he said, noting that he turned left out of his driveway when responding to a particularly traumatic fire call in 2003.

Ernie Gallant was diagnosed with PTSD after spending 20 years as a volunteer firefighter in New Glasgow, P.E.I. He says he would travel 'anywhere' to speak about his experiences with the disorder and unrecognized trauma. (Submitted by Ernie Gallant)

PTSD often presents in people who have experienced or witnessed traumatic events. Symptoms can include vivid flashbacks alongside other mental health conditions like anxiety or depression, according to the Canadian Mental Health Association.

Now, Gallant is talking publicly about his experience with PTSD. Last year, he started giving presentations that he's titled "Left Turn" in firehalls across P.E.I. to help other firefighters who may be struggling.
"Twenty-five years ago, there was nothing positive," he said.
"You went home. Best case, you sat back at the hall and talked a little bit.… Worst cases, there were guys that, [in] other halls, alcohol became an issue."
LISTEN | Former firefighter using PTSD journey to help others:
Island Morning8:09Former firefighter using PTSD journey to help others
Gallant noted that older firefighters often stand to benefit the most from talking about their experiences.
After one of his presentations in western P.E.I., Gallant said a young firefighter approached him to ask if he would speak at the fire department in Alberton.
"He said, 'I need you to come because the older members need to hear this,'" Gallant said.
"'The younger members are getting the training now but the older members aren’t.'"

items: Firefighter safety is getting more costly. Some P.E.I. stations are going into debt to keep up
Island students suiting up to fight wildfires this summer

blocks.text: Jayoda Tennekone, a registered social worker who runs a private practice in Charlottetown, said young people are generally more comfortable opening up about their mental health. He estimates that men and adolescent boys make up 80 per cent of his current caseload.
"As a generalization … younger people have that ability and the language to be able to speak about their experiences because it’s so much more normalized," Tennekone told Island Morning.
He said the men he works with often feel a need to live up to traditional stereotypes of masculinity, wanting to appear stoic and unemotional.
"That was the expectation for so long — decades and decades," he said.
"To unpack and unlearn some of that and recognize that you can be this provider, but also know when it’s time to express a level of vulnerability … it’s a challenge to get there."
LISTEN | Helping men share their feelings :
Island Morning7:33Helping men share their feelings
To speak more openly, Tennekone said men need a safe, non-judgmental space where expressing their feelings is normalized.
That’s exactly what Gallant is trying to do through his presentations: lead by example.
"It’s tough. I’m still getting better," he said.
Gallant said he would travel “anywhere” to speak about his experiences with PTSD and unrecognized trauma.
As for those who might be struggling now?
"Advocate for yourself," he said. "Don't hide."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Joseph Watt is a reporter and associate producer with CBC P.E.I. He holds a master's degree in International Journalism from City University of London. He can be reached at joseph.watt@cbc.ca
With files from Island Morning

articles.title: Robin Padilla cites bullying, suicides in call to restrict minors' social media use
articles.summary: Senator Robinhood Padilla has cited bullying, suicide cases and school shootings as reasons to restrict minors" access to social media, arguing that the problems associated with online interactions…

blocks.text: Published October 11, 2026 4:32pm

Senator Robinhood Padilla has cited bullying, suicide cases and school shootings as reasons to restrict minors’ access to social media, arguing that the problems associated with online interactions have become increasingly serious.
“ Itong panukala na ito kinakailangan itong isagawa kaagad sapagkat marami nang naidulot na hindi maganda sa ating kabataan lalo na sa mga menor de edad,” Padilla told Super Radyo dzBB on Sunday.
(The proposed measure should be implemented immediately because social media has caused many negative effects on our youth, especially minors.)
“Nandiyan ‘yung mga tinatawag nating bullying, Nagkaroon na tayo ng napakaraming suicide. Nagkaroon na tayo ng maraming mass shooting, school shooting. Lahat ‘yan patong-patong na,” he added.
(These include bullying, numerous suicide cases, and mass shootings, including school shootings. All these problems have compounded over time.)
Earlier this week, the Senate approved a bill banning minors from creating social media accounts and requiring existing accounts to be disabled or suspended.

Senate Bill 2424, or the proposed Safe Media Access and Responsible Technology for Kids in Digital Spaces (Smart Kids) Act seeks to restrict children aged 17 and below from accessing social media and other harmful digital applications and websites.
Meanwhile, the House of Representatives has approved a similar measure on second reading, but its version prohibits children aged 13 and below from creating social media accounts.
Padilla explained that the measure seeks to prevent minors aged 17 and below from engaging in social media interactions.

“Ang ipagbabawal natin sa kabataan ‘yung mayroong social media interaction, ‘yung may nakakausap. ‘Yun ‘yung problema, eh nagkakaroon tayo diyan ng kababaihan, ‘yung nude photos. Talagang sobra na eh,” he said.

(What we want to prohibit among minors is social media interaction, particularly communicating with other people. That’s where the problem lies, especially when women become victims of issues involving nude photos. It has really gone too far.)

Padilla, however, opposed the proposal to require social media platforms to obtain a franchise, saying such a requirement would be excessive and could anger the public.— Mariel Celine Serquiña/ MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Middle East crisis live: Houthis warn passengers against using Saudi airport after deadly attack on Riyadh
articles.summary:
US president Donald Trump says he is weighing whether the US will join Saudi strikes against the Iran-backed Houthis

The Houthis this morning have just also issued a warning to travellers…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 15m agoHouthis issue warning against use of Saudi airports
18m ago12 killed at Riyadh airport and hundreds wounded in Saturday strike
20m agoOpening summary

blocks.text: Houthis issue warning against use of Saudi airports
The Houthis this morning have just also issued a warning to travellers and airlines against using Saudi airports following yesterday’s attack.
It’s the first public message from the group since Saturday’s deadly assault.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said airports and airspace “are exposed to targeting and constitute a theatre of operations for our forces”, he said, adding that the group was pursuing: “airport for airport, siege for siege, and escalation for escalation”.
He said the airports in Mecca and Medina – the holiest cities in Islam- were excepted.
All week the Houthis have been striking the main international airport, which was first targeted about a fortnight ago as fighting ramped up within Yemen.

The Saudi-led coalition backing the government forces in Yemen have launched an outright offensive in the country this week to try and push back the Houthis who’ve rapidly seized and gained territory these past weeks.

The Houthis have taken over islands in the Bab al- Mandab strait and also staked stronger positions along the Red Sea, crucially seizing control of the main passageway through which its enemy state – top oil exporter Saudi Arabia- had been diverting its flows as the Strait of Hormuz remains shut off.
12 killed at Riyadh airport and hundreds wounded in Saturday strike

Saturday’s attack was the third launched on the Saudi capital’s main airport this week- with the missile making it past Saudi air defences to strike terminals 3 and 4 of King Khalid airport where hundreds of passengers were awaiting domestic flights.
The attack killed at least 12 people and injured 309 at last count, say Saudi officials.
The dead include four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese.
A projectile also fell near the King Fahd international airport in Dammam, according to the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis.
The Dammam airport has been an important alternative to Riyadh amid the recent spate of attacks.
Opening summary
Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of rapidly unfolding events in the Middle East.

After attacking Saudi Arabia’s main international airport on Saturday in strikes which killed at least 12 people and injured 309, the Houthis have issued another message this morning about the kingdom’s airports.

In response to the Houthi’s assault – the deadliest in Saudi Arabia in over a decade – US President Donald Trump has said Washington may join the Saudis in carrying out air strikes against the Iran-backed group in Yemen.
Trump said: “We may. We’re going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”

articles.title: Lacson dares Alan Cayetano: Name people I 'threatened' over Taguig infra issue
articles.summary: Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson challenged Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano to name individuals he allegedly threatened in relation to the Taguig infrastructure issue he previously flagged.

blocks.text: Published October 11, 2026 4:27pm
Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson challenged Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano to name individuals he allegedly threatened in relation to the Taguig infrastructure issue he previously flagged.
In a statement on Sunday, Lacson called Cayetano’s allegations a “tale spin” that seemed to betray his panic on the issue.

"Spinning tales betrays panic but like guilt, it will never go away. Sen. Cayetano should name the 'individuals' he alleged I threatened, so I can properly address this new issue point by point," Lacson said.
In a livestream on Saturday, Cayetano claimed to have received “feelers” that some parties were being pressured by Lacson.

“Lately, ang daming nag-send ng feelers na, ‘Sen, Kuya Alan, paano yun? Naiipit kami kasi si Senator Lacson pinipilit na may masama kahit walang makita. Tapos natuklasan nga namin na siya, staff niya, ibang kaibigan nilang lawyers, may affidavit na tapos sinusubok. Pinipilit yung iba na sila pumirma. Tapos may pananakot pa,” Cayetano said.

(Lately, a lot of people have been reaching out, saying, “Senator, Kuya Alan, what should we do? We are being pressured because Senator Lacson insists that something is wrong even though nothing has been found. Then we discovered that he, his staff, and some lawyer friends already have an affidavit and are trying to get others to sign it. There are also threats.)
Cayetano declined to elaborate but cited an alleged incident involving six contractors whom Lacson supposedly threatened with plunder charges if they refused to sign a document.
Lacson previously called for a multi-agency probe into the alleged reclamation activities in Taguig City, after flagging that the alleged illegal activities were continuing at the site.
“Tuloy-tuloy ang illegal reclamation sa Taguig side ng Laguna Lake. Somebody feels he is above the law,” Lacson said in an October 2 post on X.
(Illegal reclamation on the Taguig side of Laguna Lake continues. Somebody feels he is above the law.)

At present, Lacson said at least 45 case studies of “systematic anomalies” in flood control projects in Taguig have been submitted to the Office of the Ombudsman, which has been prompted to initiate a fact-finding investigation. —Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/RF, GMA News
