articles.title: Between adolescence and parenthood: Photo stories of Filipino teen parents
articles.summary: Through photographs, young Filipino parents offer glimpses into lives shaped by responsibilities that arrived alongside adolescence

blocks.text: “I’m a student, a worker, and a mother. Sometimes, I feel like I have three bodies.”

For this senior high school student, motherhood meant learning to carry several parts of herself all at once. Her days meant moving between school, work, and caring for her child — growing into adulthood, even while already being responsible for someone else.

This ongoing negotiation of identity, in which teens experience the push and pull of being adolescents and parents, is vividly illustrated in a new study from Ateneo de Manila University that explores through photographs — a research technique called “photovoice” — what it means to grow up while becoming a parent.

Teenage parenthood remains a pressing concern in the Philippines, with an estimated 150,000 teenage pregnancies recorded in 2022 and a 35% rise in births among girls younger than 15. Behind these statistics, studies point to gaps between existing laws and programs and teenage parents’ lived experiences, including stigma and inaccessible or irrelevant services.

Positioning teenage mothers and fathers at the center of the research process, this Ateneo study was conducted as a needs assessment to inform the development of a parenting program for teenage parents. It was designed and implemented by researchers Dr. Liane Alampay, Dr. Bernice Landoy Mamauag, and Jennel Reyes, in partnership with Masayang Pamilya Organization, Inc.

The researchers invited nine Filipino teenage parents, aged 15 to 20, from low-income communities in two provinces in Central Luzon, areas identified by the researchers’ partner organization as priorities because of their high rates of teenage pregnancy.

Through the photovoice approach, participants documented their lives by capturing or choosing images that represented their experiences and sharing the stories behind them, allowing their perspectives to inform the support and programs being developed for them.
There were no photography lessons, no tips on lighting or framing. Instead, participants were simply asked to make sure that their photographs represented something meaningful to them.

That distinction mattered. Because taking photographs was already part of the participants’ everyday lives, the method provided a familiar way to express their experiences. Some participants even used photographs symbolically rather than literally: crayons became a representation of family, while a permanent marker represented the lasting effects of sexual interactions.
What those images revealed was a life that could not be reduced to the label ‘teenage parent.’

Through their photographs, the young parents offered glimpses into lives shaped by responsibilities that arrived alongside adolescence. They spoke about uncertainty and conflict in their relationships, changes in friendships and family dynamics, and the demands of caring for a child while pursuing education or employment.

For one participant, motherhood existed alongside being a first year college student and a food server. For another, friends became family, highlighting the role of peers as a source of support and a safe space to speak openly.

Across their photographs and discussions, the researchers identified eight core themes: managing stresses and conflicts in partner relationships; peers as a source of emotional support; support and strain in family relationships; shifts in normative adolescent experiences and priorities; strain and agency in balancing roles; desire to enhance parenting knowledge and skills; environmental drivers of early sexual exposure; and sexual knowledge from social media.
Viewed through the lens of Life Course Theory, these challenges are shaped by relationship dynamics and structural norms in low-resource contexts, influencing the transition to parenthood.

The researchers found that teenage parents navigated these circumstances in different ways. Some continued their education or pursued employment, while others expressed a desire to improve how they cared for and related to their children. The researchers saw these choices as forms of agency amid the constraints they faced.Fathers and partners emerged in the narratives in contradictory ways: as sources of both stress and support.

Several mothers described conflict-laden relationships marked by imbalanced household responsibilities, financial control, and verbal and physical conflicts, tensions compounded by the adolescents’ still-developing emotional regulation capacities. Yet when fathers shared caregiving, this enabled mothers to continue their education, illustrating how paternal involvement functions as a critical resource.

The paper calls for gender-responsive strategies to bring young fathers meaningfully into support programs to strengthen family functioning, and to shift the traditional gender norms that leave adolescent mothers disproportionately bearing the burdens of early parenthood.

The Ateneo study underscored the need for accessible counseling, healthier communication and conflict resolution, and stronger support systems for young parents, alongside comprehensive sexual and reproductive health education.

At the heart of the study is the recognition that teenage parenthood is shaped by more than its challenges. It is also shaped by the relationships, circumstances, and choices through which young people find their way.
The photographs did not offer a single story of teenage parenthood — one where becoming a parent becomes the whole story of a young person’s life.

Instead, they opened a window into lives shaped by relationships, responsibilities, uncertainty, support, and choices. They revealed young people who are still growing and still finding their way while learning to care for someone else. What emerged were stories still unfolding, of young people still becoming. – Rappler.com

Nina Linly Capulong, Liane Peña Alampay, Bernice Landoy Mamauag, and Jennel Drezza Fe C. Reyes published their research, “Using Photovoice and Life Course Theory to Understand the Lived Experiences of Filipino Teenage Parents,’ in the August 2026 issue of the Journal of Research on Adolescence.

articles.title: What happens when a Google data centre comes to town? Southern India is finding out
articles.summary: India is vying to secure a piece of the AI boom, and letting Google clear hundreds of acres to build a $15 billion US data centre hub near its eastern coast. It will be the company's largest such…

image.caption: Engineering student Bali Chararan Teja, front, thought he would inherit his family's farmland — which will now be part of an AI data centre Google is building in and around Visakhapatnam, India. (Kate Kyle/CBC)

blocks.text: A group of farmers sits under the shade of a Jamun tree, chewing over the big news in their village: Google is moving in.
Google, with India's powerful Adani Group, is building a massive $15 billion US AI data centre hub in and around Visakhapatnam, a port city on India's east coast.
Farmer Bali Narasingha Rao owned one acre in Tarluvada. Pressured to sell, he says he got 17 lakhs, about $25,000, for his land — but he's unsettled about the future.
Earth movers are clearing more than 260 acres here — the biggest of three sites.
"Our land is gone, and that land was our livelihood," he said, adding that some of the village leaders told them the data centre was locating here because other countries didn’t want it.
All of a sudden his rural village is part of the AI boom.
In the race to secure a piece of it, the state government of Andhra Pradesh, has welcomed Google's five-year, multi-billion dollar investment, covering over 600 acres on three sites.
See the scale of Google's construction

At the ground-breaking ceremony in April, N. Chandrababu Naidu, the state's chief minister, said "Google is very important. If they are willing to come I'll do everything I can to extend co-operation."

The build out in this corner of India for a one-gigawatt hub is the largest for Google outside the U.S. and in many ways mirrors some concerns in other jurisdictions over water use, energy demands and noise from data centres.
"Having AI data centres is something I think India must do," said Sribharat Mathukumilli the MP for Vishakhapatnam, adding the state has big plans to attract fintech companies, banks and AI startups.
"So this is an ecosystem play. It is not a singular play."
But there is opposition from some environmental and human rights advocates, who argue the project's approvals were fast-tracked and that the costs outweigh the rewards.
Sribharat Mathukumilli, the MP for Vishakhapatnam, promotes the economic benefits of attracting data centres to India. (Kate Kyle/CBC)
"This data centre boom for us doesn't look more than a real estate project," said 26-year-old Deeksha Vanguru, a community organizer originally from Vizag, as Visakhapatnam is known.
"It is just whoever can secure the most amount of land, and slap a bunch of concrete there."
The "Stop Dirty Data Centres" campaign regularly canvasses villagers and neighbourhoods next to the three construction sites which make up Google's AI hub.
Recently Meta blocked the campaign's Instagram account under India's information technology rules.
India, Vanguru says, is fertile ground for big tech companies to expand.
"We have weak laws in terms of environmental laws, regulation laws and we give out a lot of subsidies," she said.
A municipal reservoir in Visakhapatnam shows the effects of this year's drought and weak monsoon. (Saraskanth TK/CBC)
'Huge economic value'
To attract Google, the state offered discounts on land and concessions on water and electricity tariffs for ten years.
"This is of huge economic value," said Mathukumilli, the MP. "Over time, while [Google] may have some incentives upfront, it will be a long-term economic boost."
Vanguru sees it differently.

"The central government has categorized data centres as essential infrastructures. In a country where schools are in a bad shape, where hospitals are not available," she said. "Fix the bottom foundation first."

Google's project, according to the government, could create up to 150,000 indirect jobs in related tech industries, and 4,000 a year during construction. But running the data centres will require only hundreds of permanent employees; many of those will be service jobs to maintain the facilities, argue opponents.
Demonstrators march against the Google hub in Visakhapatnam, on Sept. 19. Activists regularly canvass villagers and neighbourhoods next to the three construction sites. (Kate Kyle/CBC)
'Completely unhappy'
In the rural village of Tarluvada, just outside Visakhapatnam, a group of young men approach CBC News.
"We‘re talking [for] our village members, ma'am,” said 23-year-old Bali Charan Teja. ”We are completely unhappy with the data centre."

Local farmer Bali Narasingha Rao, left, was persuaded to sell his one acre of land for the data centre. It was the only land he'd ever owned and now he worries about the next generation. (Kate Kyle/CBC)
"It's a data storage centre, useful for only storage or cooling of the systems so I can't believe that we can get any employment here."
He's studying to be a civil engineer and thought he would inherit his family's farm land — now sold off — as part of his legacy.
Nearby in Vizag, some residents are worried the data centre will use up too much water.
A weak monsoon and drought this year have stretched water resources. The local reservoir has receded and ground water is dropping.
Area resident V. Jyothi says she welcomes the potential new jobs, but worries about the water shortages already plaguing her part of Visakhapatnam. (Kate Kyle/CBC)
"The water problem has become very serious," said V. Jyothi, standing in front of her modest two-room home.
"We know that the data centre is coming, and we have heard that it could lead to water problems."
Air cooling system
The state government says water will not be diverted from residential use, but people are skeptical.

Google, in an email statement to CBC News, says it will use an "advanced air cooling system," in place of water cooling, "limiting water consumption​" to primarily restrooms and kitchens. It says the facility is designed to keep "boundary sound" outside the data centre "below 55 decibels … roughly the volume of a dishwasher."

A court challenge in August failed to halt work on the data centre hub, parts of which are scheduled to be operational in 2028. Google is also laying three subsea cables for data connectivity off the Visakhapatnam coast.

On the beach Sudeep Pillarisetty, a software developer and entrepreneur, is excited that Google chose his city for a data centre, confident it will kick off data science and engineering roles for young tech professionals.

Could AI really 'kill all humans'? Breaking down the dire warnings about the technology's existential risk
How AI could usher in a 'new scientific golden age' — if it doesn't kill us all first

blocks.text: "I hope Google provides a subsidy for any of the Indian startups to create their own AI models — made in India," he said.
But in the village on the bench under the tree, the farmers are still debating the merits.
"This land is the only livelihood and security we have for our children, " said Bali Sanyasa Rao.
"We will know whether it is beneficial or harmful only after the data centre is completed."

articles.title: 'You're Russian now': Ukrainians raised in Crimea share how Russia trained them to become future soldiers
articles.summary: Three Ukrainians who grew up in occupied Crimea describe how Russia trained them to become future soldiers for its war on Ukraine, including school classes on how to handle weapons — part of a larger…
articles.byline: Aloysius Wong, Terence McKenna, Alex Shprintsen

image.caption: From left, Ukrainians Daria Tomashova, Matvii Chos and Daria Fursova grew up in Russian-occupied Crimea, where they describe being subjected to indoctrination and forced to do military training. They have each shared their experiences with the international community at conferences and the United Na

blocks.text: Growing up in Crimea under Russian occupation, Matvii Chos feared he would be drafted into the Russian army as soon as he became an adult.

"If you're a man and you turn 18 years old, they almost immediately draft you," said Chos, 19, who enrolled at a Moscow university to avoid conscription and later escaped Russia with the help of a Ukrainian non-profit.

But he says the brainwashing and militarization started much earlier. Chos says they began having special cadet classes in 2020, when he was a sixth-grade student. They were trained in a range of military techniques — loading and reloading weapons, marching, tactical medicine — a co-ordinated effort, Chos says, to create future soldiers to fight his fellow Ukrainians.
"What Russia is doing is occupying territories, kidnapping children and turning them [into] Russian soldiers," he said.
Russia kidnapping, brainwashing children to be future soldiers, says Ukrainian teen

Fifty countries signed a pledge at the Pathways to Peace international conference held in Toronto on Sept. 29, expressing concern about the militarization of children in occupied territories and calling for the “immediate, safe and unconditional return” of Ukrainian children forcibly transferred into Russia.

The indoctrination and forced military training Chos was subjected to is an experience shared by many Ukrainian youth in territories controlled by Russia — an issue especially urgent, human rights experts say, because of how vulnerable children are.
"Childhood has an expiration date," said Oleksandra Matviichuk, a Ukrainian human rights lawyer who heads the Center for Civil Liberties, which won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2022.
"The children from occupied territories, they're losing their childhood. We lose these children."
Speaking Ukrainian forbidden
Other young Ukrainians who spoke to CBC News outlined the various ways Russian culture and values were imposed on them as children.
Daria Fursova, 23, remembers how quickly her elementary school curriculum changed after Russia annexed Crimea in 2014 when she was 11.
"The administration said that there will no longer be Ukrainian books in school, in classes," she said, recalling the start of fifth grade.
How Russia justifies its invasion of Ukraine to children in occupied Crimea
Not long after, Fursova’s school stopped teaching Ukrainian and instead began instructing them in Russian history and the Russian language.

Speaking Ukrainian and Crimean Tatar — a language considered "highly endangered" by UNESCO — was forbidden, even during breaks, according to 18-year-old Daria Tomashova, who says the indoctrination was "everywhere," from textbooks in school to what was broadcast on TV.
Chos has similar memories of the sudden shift after the occupation.
"We started to learn [the] Russian anthem at school, learn Russian songs, learn Russian poems," he said. "They said to us, 'You're Russian now. You lived all of your life in Russia.' "

Fursova left Crimea to study in Kyiv in 2021 before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, but says the situation in Crimea has since become "way worse." Her old school posted lessons on social media defending the war, and she says many of her former classmates have since joined the Russian army.
Daria Fursova, 23, shares her experience growing up in occupied Crimea at the United Nations General Assembly on Sept. 23, during the sixth summit of the Crimea Platform. (UN Web TV)
20,000 children abducted

Beyond the Russification of occupied Crimea, the international community has raised particular concern with how Russia has forcibly separated tens of thousands of Ukrainian children from their families and taken them into Russian territory — an act Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as "mass kidnapping" amounting to genocide.

Many of those children have shared stories of abuse while in Russian custody, including being placed in isolation cells for not being co-operative in Russian re-education camps. Other children are given new identities, naturalized as Russian citizens and forcibly adopted into foster families in Russia.
The children abducted by Putin’s war machine
Ukrainian officials estimate that Russia has unlawfully deported 20,000 children since the invasion began in February 2022. Of those, only about 2,650 have been returned so far.
The co-ordinated campaign has led to charges at the International Criminal Court against Russian President Vladimir Putin and Children’s Rights Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova.

items: Ukrainian children abducted by Russia appeal for help from Canadian MPs

blocks.text: Minister of Foreign Affairs Anita Anand says she holds Putin personally responsible for the policies that have led to Ukrainian children being "stolen" from their families.

"My hope is that we ensure the full return of all Ukrainian children, and every single person who has committed an injustice in stealing these children face the consequences that international law requires," Anand said in an interview with CBC.
Canada committed to bringing Ukrainian children home: Anand
Children just want to return to 'normal life'

Anand says Canada has committed nearly $7 million to support organizations that work to bring Ukrainian children home and fund psychological support for the trauma endured as a result of the "indoctrination, militarization and essentially the Russian attempt to convert these Ukrainian children into members of Russia’s war machine."
One of those organizations is Save Ukraine, a charity that identifies kidnapped children and conducts operations to rescue them.

Its founder, Mykola Kuleba, says he is grateful for Canada’s leadership on the issue, but emphasized how critical the present situation is, with some young Ukrainians now presumably fighting as Russian soldiers and dying on the battlefield.
'Long way' to justice and accountability for abducted Ukrainian kids, says NGO founder

"We should understand that we're running out of time for these children, and we're losing every day someone who's taken forcibly to the Russian army," said Kuleba, the former commissioner for children’s rights in Ukraine.
Kuleba says the children they bring home tell him they just want to live in peace with their families in their hometowns.
"They want [to] survive. They want to return to a normal life. They want to stay with their loved ones."

items: 'We need strong support': Ukraine fighting to bring children back from Russia
There can be no peace with Russia until Ukrainian children come home, says advocate

blocks.text: Chos was eventually able to escape Russia with the help of Save Ukraine, which gave him food, shelter, mental health support and documentation.

But the process was nerve-racking: Chos had to travel to the Ukrainian consulate in Belarus twice, and said if Russian authorities had searched him and found anything suggesting he was pro-Ukraine, he would be facing over a decade in Russian prison.

Chos, left, and Tomashova speak at the Pathways to Peace international conference in Toronto on Sept. 28. The Ukrainian couple fell in love and married after being rescued by Save Ukraine, a non-profit that identifies kidnapped children and conducts operations to get them to safety. (Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press)
Now a married couple, Chos and Tomashova shared their experiences at the recent international conference in Toronto.
"I managed to escape," Chos told the room of delegates, "but a lot of children are still left there."

articles.title: Sara Duterte regrets alleged PH link to illegal drugs seized in Thailand, Laos
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte expressed regret on Sunday over the country"s alleged involvement in the illegal drugs seized recently in Thailand and Laos.

blocks.text: Published October 11, 2026 3:55pm
Vice President Sara Duterte expressed regret on Sunday over the country’s alleged involvement in the illegal drugs seized recently in Thailand and Laos.
Foreign authorities said the illegal drugs intercepted in the two countries were both bound for the Philippines.

“We also acknowledge the challenges our own country faces in addressing the illegal drug trade. We recognize the concerns surrounding the Philippines’ role in regional drug trafficking and express my deep regret that our country has become associated with this problem,” Duterte said in a statement.
The Vice President likewise extended her gratitude to Thai and Laotian governments for “saving many Filipino families” from the impact of narcotics.

“I extend my sincere appreciation to the governments of Laos and Thailand for their continued efforts and firm commitment to combating illegal drug trafficking and strengthening regional security,” Duterte said.
“Their actions have helped save many Filipino families from the devastating effects of illegal drugs and have contributed to safer communities across the Philippines,” she added.
On October 7, the South China Morning Post reported that 521 kilograms of suspected methamphetamine were seized from a private jet in Laos. The drugs were allegedly bound for Manila.

The following day, the Bangkok Post reported the interception of more than a ton of crystal methamphetamine worth 1.2 billion baht (approximately P2.2 billion) from a boat in the Gulf of Thailand, which was reportedly being transported to the Philippines as well.
The Philippine National Police (PNP) said that it has been coordinating with foreign authorities to verify the reports.

"We are glad na hindi na nakarating po dito sa ating itong mga droga na ito. But as to the claim na ito po talaga ay destined for the country, it's premature to conclude whether it's true or not," PNP spokesperson Police Colonel Allen Rae Co said
(We are glad that these drugs have not reached our country. But as for the claim that this is really destined for the country, it's premature to conclude whether it is true or not.)

In her statement, Duterte pointed to the Philippines’ membership in ASEAN and committed to strengthening the country’s law enforcement efforts, regional intelligence-sharing, and cooperation with neighboring countries to combat drug trafficking.
She said the Philippines pledges to work toward “a safer and more secure Southeast Asia for all.” —Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/RF, GMA News

articles.title: Missing Australian hiker Jordan Yap last seen on remote trail found dead in Peru
articles.summary:
Family and friends say Melbourne man should be remembered for ‘immense joy he brought to so many people’s lives’

  • Get our

blocks.text: An Australian trekker who was last seen on a remote South American hiking trail has been found dead, his family have said.
Jordan Yap, 30, last made contact with friends and family on 14 September ahead of a planned 10-day solo trek along Peru’s Huayhuash mountain range, 400km north-east of Lima.
In a social media post on Saturday, his friends and family said “with a heavy heart we are sorry to tell you Jordan has been found, and he did not survive”.

“We want to thank everyone who has helped; friends and family, the contributors, the search teams, the police, the many groups we engaged with who gave their time and effort, everyone who helped to share on social media. We are appreciative of all of you.
“Please remember Jordan as the vibrant man he was, and for the immense joy he brought to so many people’s lives.
“Rest in peace Jordan – from your friends and family.”

The Melbourne man was last seen near the beginning of his trek across the Cordillera Huayhuash circuit, which is regarded as a challenging, high-altitude trek through the remote Andes mountains. His friends and family regarded him as a very experienced hiker.

His friends and family became concerned after he failed to make contact on his estimated return date, failed to check back into the Krusty hostel in Huaraz and missed a scheduled flight from Lima to Cusco.
The avid trekker misplaced a satellite beacon he was travelling with days before he set off on the 120km hike, raising further concerns.

articles.title: Surrogacy in Georgia is booming, but at what cost?
articles.summary: Georgia became a hub for surrogate pregnancies after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. DW spoke with parents, and those who wanted to become parents, about the hidden costs of a…

image.caption: After Russia's invasion of Ukraine, much of the surrogacy industry shifted to GeorgiaImage: SWR

blocks.text: Three years ago, Olga, 40, and Daniel (both names changed to protect the their identities) from Hamburg decided to employ the services of a surrogate mother. But surrogacy is illegal in Germany, and people whose children are born through surrogacy must pursue the legal recognition of their parenthood in German courts.

Olga is a German citizen, but was born and raised in Russia. That's why the couple wanted to learn more about the surrogacy market in Russia. But foreign customers have been banned from signing Russian surrogacy contracts since 2022. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, many international agencies that liaise between surrogates and intended parents moved to Georgia. So, Olga and Daniel traveled there.
Georgia the new destination for surrogate mothers

In the past years, Georgia, a mountainous country in the Caucasus region, has become a sort of surrogacy hub, with women traveling from all over the world to work as surrogates. According to Georgia's Public Service Development Agency, over 3,000 surrogate mothers were registered in 2023 across the country. Since 2012, they've given birth to over 5,000 children. And since the beginning of Russia's war in Ukraine, the number of children born to surrogate mothers has skyrocketed. While an estimated 300 surrogate mothers gave birth in 2021, that number leapt to over 1,100 by 2023.

Anastasia, 39, is a surrogate mother from Russia working in Georgia. She has a grown daughter and has already seen through three surrogate pregnancies. Her first was in 2021, which she used to finance a property down payment.
Surrogacy in the US: a different path to parenthood

Anastasia says she completed her first two surrogacies in Russia, and her third — for a Japanese couple, brokered through the branch office of a Moscow clinic — in Georgia. Like many surrogate mothers, she went home to Russia after the embryo was implanted, and returned to Georgia when she was 22 weeks pregnant.

"I live in an apartment with another surrogate mother who carried twins to term. This program was the easiest and most practical one for me, but maybe I just got lucky with the right clinic," Anastasia told DW. "Other women who gave birth in Georgia told me they had difficulties. For example, after giving birth, they had to wait a long time before they were paid." She says she's ready to become a surrogate mother again.

Estimates vary, but there are about 19 clinics that offer such services across Georgia. And at around €45,000 ($50,400) to €55,000, the average service costs for agencies in Tbilisi or Batumi are only about a third of what agencies in other countries charge.
Several surrogate mothers who gave birth in Georgian clinics told DW that their average salary was between €18,000 and €28,000, with premiums added for birthing twins, for example.
Surrogate mothers from Ukraine in demand

Daniel and Olga told DW that they spent months looking for surrogacy agency in Georgia. "Pretty soon, we had access to a list of women from Russia, Ukraine, Kazakhstan, and Georgia, and were given a detailed description of the process, along with the contact information of lawyers who could help take care of the formalities," they recount. "We were a little concerned that not every agency could give clear answers about the health of some of the surrogate mothers."

Both work in the medical field, and Olga says perhaps some of their questions about the physical health and possible genetic disorders might have been too probing. "We picked a 30-year-old woman from Ukraine who had already been a surrogate mother once for a European couple," she says. The Russian-Georgian agency set up half-hour long Zoom call, "but that hardly seemed enough to make a final decision," Olga adds.

In the spring of 2024, the married couple traveled to Georgia's capital to meet Elena (her name has been changed to protect her identity). Following a long discussion, the agency had seemed reluctant when they agreed to bring her to Tbilisi for the meeting. Elena made a good first impression on the couple from Hamburg, showing them pictures of her children and telling them she wanted to use the money she earned to renovate her apartment.

"They had initially told us that the surrogate would spent the entire pregnancy living in a rented apartment in Tbilisi," Olga and Daniel tell DW. "But then we found out that Elena was going back home for a few months after the embryo was implanted, back to Ukraine, where there's war."
Human rights experts criticize legislation

Georgian laws have a weak spot, the human rights lawyer Nino Bogveradze tells DW: They only regulate the relationship between the surrogate mothers, the intended parents, and the clinics, but they do not consider the roles that agencies play.

In Georgia, surrogate mothers have limited rights. Most concerns related to their pregnancy, medical care or payment are not regulated by national law but in contracts between the involved parties. And the state does not set minimum standards for social guarantees or contractual terms.
Surrogacy laws and rules vary widely across Africa

After an embryo has been implanted, surrogate mothers are not allowed to keep the child, leave the program, or end the pregnancy. Several human rights groups, including Human Rights Watch and the International Women's Health Coalition say the established practice in Georgia violates women's rights to reproductive self-determination.
Agencies guided by material interests

"Agencies often speak of their special mission to help people have the child they've been dreaming of," Olga Doletskaya from the University of Leeds tell DW. "But in reality, they're primarily driven by financial interests. And that's why they exploit the precarious situation of surrogate mothers, and pressure intended parents."

Olga and Daniel from Hamburg agree. "We were constantly being made to understand that we should decide as quickly as possible. We had to hurry because apparently several other couples were also interested in our surrogate," Olga says.

And the agency kept stressing that it had paid out of pocket for bringing the potential surrogate mother to Georgia, despite that not being contractually agreed. "At some point, a representative noticed my emotional state and asked me how long I wanted to remain childless," Olga recounts. "I felt like I was being manipulated."
The couple returned to Germany with mixed feelings and decided to shelve the idea of employing a surrogate mother — at least, for now.
Mark Sheider and Asja Lokina contributed to this article, which originally appeared in Russian.

articles.title: Where is Robin Padilla really from? Senator explains
articles.summary: Senator Robinhood Padilla on Sunday explained his family's roots and ties to different parts of the Philippines after netizens questioned where he actually hails from.

blocks.text: Published October 11, 2026 3:23pm
Senator Robinhood Padilla on Sunday explained his family's roots and ties to different parts of the Philippines after netizens questioned where he actually hails from.
In an interview on Super Radyo dzBB, Padilla said his family had moved from one place to another over several generations, even tracing its roots to Spain.

“Ang Padilla talaga ay travelers from Spain. Napunta ’yan sa Pilipinas. Noong una, pumunta kami sa Maynila. Nagkagulo sa Pangasinan, napunta yung mga Padilla sa Nueva Ecija hanggang sa napunta sa Bulacan," Padilla said.

(The Padillas were originally travelers from Spain who came to the Philippines. They initially settled in Manila. Following unrest in Pangasinan, the Padillas moved to Nueva Ecija and eventually to Bulacan.)
"Yung tatay ko talaga Camarines Norte, ako po ay nag-aral sa Baguio. Ang nanay ko taga-Abra, ang lola ko taga-Abra, kaya talaga ako po ay kalat,” he added.
(My father was from Camarines Norte, while I studied in Baguio. My mother and grandmother were from Abra, so I have connections to many places.)
“Hanggang Mindanao, hanggang Visayas may Padilla (There are Padillas even in Mindanao and the Visayas),” he added.

Padilla, who is serving as a senator-judge in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, recently drew attention on social media after repeatedly citing different places he had lived while questioning prosecution witnesses.
His remarks prompted netizens to wonder where he actually originated.
Responding to the online reactions, Padilla said his extensive travels across the country had allowed him to establish connections with communities, including indigenous peoples in remote areas.
“Wala silang magagawa, talagang si Robin Padilla, talagang ako po ay matatawag na traveler. Ako po ay talagang kalat sa bayan natin, kahit sa kasulok-sulukang bundok," the senator said.
(There is nothing critics can do about it. I can truly be called a traveler. I have been all over the country, even in the remotest mountain communities.)
"Kapag may nakausap na mga katutubo, sasabihin na taga-dito si Robin Padilla,”
If you talk to Indigenous people, they would say Robin Padilla is from their area.)— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Germany's population is shrinking, but not everywhere
articles.summary: By 2045, Germany will have more older people, fewer workers and a smaller population overall. Yet some regions will defy this trend. Their success depends on how much they have to offer.

image.caption: Some areas in Germany will see population numbers dwindleImage: Jens Kalaene/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Germany's population is expected to decline from 83.5 million in 2025 to around 81.8 million by 2045, according to a new study from the Berlin Institute for Population and Development (Berlin-Institut für Bevölkerung und Entwicklung), in collaboration with the Wüstenrot Foundation, a non-profit that supports research on housing, urban development, and social change.

The decline in population alone is not the central challenge. More significant is the continuing rise in the number of retirees alongside a steadily shrinking workforce. Across Germany, the working-age population is projected to decrease by 4.7% by 2045.

"The baby boomer generation is retiring, while significantly smaller cohorts are following. Birth rates are falling, and immigration is not sufficient to offset the growing surplus of deaths over births," said Institute President Catherina Hinz when presenting the study in Berlin.
The term "baby boomers" refers to those born in the 1960s, when annual births exceeded one million. Thereafter, the birth rate fell sharply, effectively halving.
The economy matters

Germany's population may be shrinking, but according to the study, this trend is far from uniform across the country. In the years ahead, a region's economic attractiveness, and the financial strength that comes with it, will become even more important than it is today.

"Some regions will lose substantial numbers of residents and workers in the years ahead, while others continue to grow. Even within eastern Germany, southern Germany, and rural areas, the demographic and economic divide is widening," said Hinz.

"Demographic change is unfolding before our very eyes, and its effects are being felt across the country," Hinz added. "Its consequences can still be mitigated, but they can no longer be avoided. And the longer we wait, the narrower our scope for action will become."

Hinz's warning is echoed by Frederick Sixtus of the Berlin Institute. Almost every region now records more deaths than births, he notes, a consequence of decades of low birth rates. The implication is clear: Migration, both inward and outward, now shapes a region's demographic trajectory. Over recent decades, immigration from abroad has repeatedly helped stabilize population trends. Yet migration alone is no longer enough to halt the aging of society.

According to the study, several factors are critical if a region is to remain attractive to people relocating from abroad or from other parts of Germany: High-quality jobs offering good pay and working conditions, a sufficient supply of skilled workers for local businesses, financially robust municipalities, reliable childcare, and efficient transport and mobility infrastructure.
Berlin leads the way

Many major cities are expected to continue to grow in the years ahead, according to Manuel Slupina of the Wüstenrot Foundation. The study projects that Berlin will lead the way, with the capital's population increasing by almost 10% by 2045. Other cities expected to attract people include Hamburg, Frankfurt am Main, Munich, and Düsseldorf in western Germany, as well as Leipzig, Dresden, and Potsdam in the east.

The study's authors argue that the familiar distinction between urban and rural areas does not hold true everywhere. The hinterlands of many major cities are also expected to grow. While young people are increasingly drawn to metropolitan centers, families with children tend to settle in the surrounding areas. Among the places likely to lose population are several large cities in western Germany, including Bremen, Duisburg, Dortmund, and Kaiserslautern, whose economic appeal has gradually diminished. At the bottom of the ranking are many sparsely populated regions, a large number of them in eastern Germany.
Competition for talent

Twelve of the 20 districts and independent cities with the weakest overall ratings are now located in eastern Germany, up from five in the previous assessment in 2019. According to the study, these regions are also expected to see the steepest declines in their working-age populations, with losses of up to 18% by 2045. The authors conclude that competition for workers is therefore set to become one of the key demographic challenges of the decades ahead.

In this competition, the southern German states of Bavariaand Baden-Württemberg are regarded as having the strongest prospects. Bavaria ranks particularly highly thanks to its robust economy, which is thriving across much of the state, and its strong labor market. Women, older people, and people without German citizenship are also more likely to be employed in Bavaria than elsewhere. The ranking shows that economically successful regions are more effective at integrating different population groups into the labor market than weaker ones.
Why Germans want children but are having fewer babies
Policymakers must find local solutions
Under Germany's constitution, the country is committed to ensuring that people enjoy comparable opportunities, and with them the prospect of a good life, regardless of where they live.

The researchers offer clear recommendations to policymakers. They argue that the focus must be on addressing structural challenges and regional disparities. "What may be the right response for a growing major city is not necessarily the right one for a shrinking rural district," says Slupina. Tailor-made solutions are needed, but they require the right framework conditions. "There needs to be less rigid regulation, more scope for local initiative, and greater financial resources, especially for municipalities and those actively engaged at the local level." Slupina's message is clear: Regions should be trusted to shape their own futures.

Local authorities would no doubt welcome that. For years, mayors and district administrators have been calling for greater financial autonomy. They are currently seeking a larger share of overall tax revenues for municipalities. The federal government and the states, however, argue that they face budgetary constraints of their own. Yet both sides recognize that, sooner or later, Germany will have little choice but to reform its system of fiscal federalism.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: ‘It was a terrible thing’: Panama declares state of emergency as quake aftershocks rattle communities
articles.summary:
More than 100 aftershocks as high as magnitude-5.8 recorded after two quakes toppled buildings and prompted evacuations

Panama’s government has declared a state of emergency on Saturday as…

blocks.text: Panama’s government has declared a state of emergency on Saturday as the aftershocks of two powerful earthquakes that roiled the country shook communities for hours.
Officials did not attribute any deaths to Friday’s 7.7- and 6.6-magnitude earthquakes, but reported damages in all 10 of Panama’s provinces and two Indigenous territories.

The earthquakes toppled buildings near the epicentre and prompted evacuations across the Central American country. Seismologists recorded more than 100 aftershocks, including ones measuring magnitude 5.8, 5.5 and 5.2.

The earlier quake, also felt in neighbouring Colombia, was centred about 10km (6 miles) south-west of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, in the central province of Herrera, according to the US Geological Survey. It struck at a depth of 10km (6 miles).

blocks.caption: A car sits crushed beneath debris from a collapsed building in Penonome, Panama. Photograph: Enea Lebrun/Reuters

blocks.text: The presidential minister, Juan Carlos Orillac, announced the emergency during a news conference in the capital, Panama City. He said homes, schools, healthcare facilities, roads and hotels were among the damaged facilities.
Malitzie Rivera, the deputy director of the National Civil Protection System, said 27 people had been reported with injuries, ranging from minor to moderate.
Most of the damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera, Cocle and Los Santos.

About 420 homes and the same number of public schools had been damaged, according to the Civil Protection agency. It also reported that seven hotels, at least 13 churches and nine bridges were affected by the earthquakes.

In La Villa de Los Santos, a colonial-era community about 64km (40 miles) north-east of the epicentre, homes and a historical Catholic church collapsed. People who spent the night on the streets were waiting for the government’s guidance on what to do next.

“We’ve been here since 1 pm yesterday; we haven’t moved,” Tony Jiménez, whose home partially collapsed, said, while sitting with relatives under a tent. “It was a terrible thing. I can tell you with absolute certainty that in my 90 years, I had never experienced anything like it. It was intense – truly intense.”

blocks.caption: Elodia Oliva (94) rests in a park in downtown Tonosi, Panama, on Saturday.  Photograph: Bienvenido Velasco/EPA

blocks.text: Officials did not report any missing people on Saturday but said some communities remained cut off due to landslides and road damage.

That the country appeared to have avoided widespread deaths could be due to its strict building codes, especially governing the construction of skyscrapers in the capital, said Carlos Valdés, the head of the seismology department at the National Autonomous University of Mexico.

Messages of support and offers of assistance were sent from across the region shortly after the earthquakes. Mulino on Friday thanked fellow Latin American leaders for their support, saying he had spoken with the presidents of Chile, Uruguay and Guatemala, among others.

The US Department of State on Saturday said it mobilised a disaster response team to help local authorities with search and rescue expertise as well as aerial and on-the-ground assessments. The US government also pledged $5m for humanitarian assistance.
The US military’s southern command said two helicopters, supported by the state department’s drug-control bureau, had delivered 2,000 pounds (907kg) of food to people affected by the earthquakes.

articles.title: Marcos eyes deeper technology ties with Singapore
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said he is hoping that the Philippines and Singapore will enter into new partnerships, particularly in technology, once he steps down from office in 2028.

blocks.text: Published October 11, 2026 2:46pm
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said he is hoping that the Philippines and Singapore will enter into new partnerships, particularly in technology, once he steps down from office in 2028.
The Philippine leader noted that Singapore is leading the way when it comes to artificial intelligence (AI) in Southeast Asia.

“Hopefully by then, we will have entered into partnerships in the new areas that are becoming, the new opportunities that are being made available to us by the advent of new technology,” said Marcos in an interview with The Straits Times during his five-day work visit to the city-state.

“Of course, the biggest discussions now are being held over AI and Singapore has an important part to play in that because Singapore is actually, in our region, an industry leader when it comes to digitalization and AI,” he added.
Marcos earlier said that his visit to Singapore from October 7 to 11 would help prepare the Philippines for the industries of the future.
The President also said this latest working visit will build upon his previous trip to the country last July, where he engaged investors in digital infrastructure, AI, healthcare, and more.

“Singapore has been one of the biggest investors in the Philippines already. They have been very focused in the areas that they had wanted to develop but now we are exploring new areas, even areas such as health care, of course the digital economy, infrastructure, which is generally, traditionally, Singapore has not been involved before but they are coming into that now in the Philippines,” he told the Singaporean newspaper.
“This is a very, very important development for us and I think it's also of great benefit to Singapore,” Marcos added. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Marcos rejects claims of PH 'aggression' in WPS
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has rejected claims that the Philippines has been aggressive in its dealings with China amid continuing tensions in the West Philippine Sea, saying the country has only…

blocks.text: Published October 11, 2026 2:30pm

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has rejected claims that the Philippines has been aggressive in its dealings with China amid continuing tensions in the West Philippine Sea, saying the country has only been defending its territory and sovereign rights.
“We have never been aggressive in any way whatsoever,” Marcos said in an interview with The Straits Times during his five-day working visit to Singapore.
Marcos maintained that the Philippines was merely exercising its rights and protecting its territory, rejecting suggestions that its actions had contributed to tensions in the disputed waters.

“To say aggressive, aggressive is to go out and initiate some kind of conflict. We have never done that. We are there, we are sitting in our country, and all we do is defend our rights, defend our territory,” he said.

In 2016, an international arbitral tribunal in The Hague ruled in favor of the Philippines, invalidating China's sweeping claims over much of the South China Sea for having no legal basis under international law. Beijing has refused to recognize the ruling.
The Philippines lodged 296 diplomatic protests against China from 2022 to 2026, including 39 so far this year, according to the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA).

“So no, we have not been aggressive at all. We have been the point at which aggression is felt (more) than (in) any other country in the region. So I can assure you the aggression does not come from the Philippines,” Marcos said.
Marcos' remarks came amid continued reports of Chinese harassment of Philippine vessels in the West Philippine Sea.

In one of the latest incidents, the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) reported that Chinese Coast Guard vessels obstructed and delayed the emergency medical evacuation of a Philippine Navy personnel from Ayungin Shoal.
Chinese vessels also reportedly interfered with a Philippine resupply mission to Ayungin Shoal on September 24, prompting condemnation from the United States Embassy in Manila.
The incidents were among the latest confrontations between Philippine and Chinese vessels in the disputed waters, where Beijing continues to assert its expansive maritime claims.

Despite the tensions, Marcos expressed openness to pursuing joint oil exploration with China, provided that both countries could agree on commercial arrangements without compromising their respective positions on territorial disputes.
Asked whether the Philippines remained willing to undertake joint oil exploration with Beijing, Marcos replied: “Yes, I absolutely do. I don't see why we cannot do that.”

“It is something that I think both countries would like to pursue and I think that if we keep it at a purely commercial level and do not enter into territorial conflicts and a resolution of who owns what and who belongs where, what law will apply,” he said.
“So long as we can come to an agreement on that and I don't see why we should not be able to have that partnership,” he added.
In August, Marcos said there was no definite timeline for the possible resumption of joint oil exploration talks between Manila and Beijing.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Robin Padilla, allied senators may skip Duterte impeachment trial over 'disregard for law'
articles.summary: Senator Robin Padilla on Sunday said he and his allied senators may skip the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte should there be what he described as disregard for the law.

blocks.text: Published October 11, 2026 2:26pm
Senator Robin Padilla on Sunday said he and his allied senators may skip the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte should there be what he described as disregard for the law.
Padilla told Super Radyo dzBB that senators in the minority bloc have not discussed skipping the impeachment trial, but such talks may happen soon.
“Wala pong ganoong usapan pero baka malapit na po (There has been no such discussion yet, but it may happen soon),” Padilla said.

He also opposed the Senate impeachment court’s ruling that the two-thirds voting threshold should be based on the number of senators who are “legally and factually participating in the impeachment proceedings.”

“Marami po kasing kagulat-gulat na mga nangyayari. Huwag na po nating i-identify kung na minority, majority kasi hindi maganda kapag impeachment tapos kami ay namomolitika pa. Kami po na naniniwala na sundin ang saligang batas,” Padilla said.

(There have been many surprising developments. Let us not identify whether we belong to the minority or majority bloc because it would not look good if we were seen as engaging in politics while an impeachment trial is ongoing. We believe in upholding the Constitution.)
“Ayaw naming mabaluktot ang batas. Kapag hindi tumigil ang pagbabaluktot ng batas ay baka baka dumating na punto na hindi na kami umattend,” he added.
(We do not want the law to be twisted. If this continues, there may come a point when we will no longer attend the proceedings.)
Earlier this week, Padilla and Senator Christopher “Bong” Go filed a petition asking the Supreme Court to declare null the Senate’s impeachment country’s ruling on the voting threshold.

In a petition for certiorari and prohibition, the senators and the Partido Demokratiko Pilipino-Lakas ng Bayan (PDP-Laban) asked the SC to issue a status quo ante order or a temporary restraining order directing the Impeachment court and the House of Representatives to refrain from excluding any senator from the count of “all members of the Senate” under the Constitution.
“The Constitution does not count only the Senators it finds convenient. It says ‘all,’ and ‘all’ has never meant ‘some.” Two-thirds of twenty-four is sixteen,” the petitioners said.
Villar joins majority bloc
On Thursday, Senator Mark Villar moved from the minority to the majority bloc after the Senate elected him to the Commission on Appointments and as chairman of the Senate Committee on Public Works.
For Padilla, the change should be seen in a positive light.
“Sa totoo lang po, sa ganitong bagay, kailangan positive ka lagi. Kasi masyado ng negative ang politika,” Padilla said.
(To be honest, in matters like this, you have to remain positive because politics has become too negative.)
“‘Yung paglipat ni (Senator) Mark (Villar) bilang legislative senator ‘yun. Hindi siya as senator-judge kasi diyan naman sa pagiging senator-judge wala namang minority, majority diyan,” he added.
(Senator Mark Villar’s transfer was in his capacity as a legislative senator, not as a senator-judge, because there is no minority or majority bloc in the impeachment court.)
Following the development, the majority bloc is now composed of 14 members, while the minority has 10 members — four of whom are currently not attending sessions.

Currently, Senators Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta are detained over separate plunder charges, Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa is in hiding amid an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court, and Senator Loren Legarda has been absent for weeks due to health concerns and is currently abroad.
Padilla hoped that the minority bloc would not lose more members following Villar’s transfer.

“Wala pang nagpapaalam. Sana wala naman pero hindi naman namin ikasasama ng loob ‘yan kasi katunayan ho kakaunti lang naman talaga kaming nag-umpisang minority diyan. Sila lang naman ‘yung lumipat sa amin. So, hindi naman,” Padilla said.

(No one has informed us of any plans to leave. I hope no one does, but we will not take it against them because, in fact, we were only a few when we initially formed the minority bloc. They were the ones who later joined us.)—RF, GMA News

articles.title: Trump calls for replacing Ukraine’s Zelenskyy in tussle over diesel deal with Russia
articles.summary: 'I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president,' US President Donald Trump says

blocks.text: 'I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president,' US President Donald Trump says

US President Donald Trump on Saturday, October 11, called for Ukraine to replace its leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy and railed against Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil infrastructure, a day after announcing a diesel supply deal with Russia that had drawn a sharp rebuke from Zelenskyy.

In some of his harshest criticism yet of the White House, Zelenskyy linked the US lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel with a Russian attack on Saturday, October 10, that killed 20 people, including 3 children, in the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia.

A steep rise in global diesel prices, which followed the outbreak of the Iran war in February, has become a political liability for Trump’s Republican Party ahead of next month’s midterm elections, when opposition Democrats could gain control of one or both houses of Congress.
“I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” Trump told reporters at the White House, saying Zelenskyy had hurt global diesel supplies with strikes on Russian refineries.
“He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel because Russia supplies a large portion of the diesel fuel throughout the world.”
Zelenskyy says diesel deal emboldens Russia

Earlier in the day, ZelZelenskyyensky said Trump’s announcement on Friday of the diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin had emboldened Moscow. Kyiv has instead urged Washington to pressure Moscow for serious negotiations to end the 4-1/2-year-old war.
The Russian government said on Saturday it had partially lifted a ban on diesel exports.
“Today, Russia said thank you for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelenskyy said.

“Last night provided yet more confirmation that Russia perceives any easing of pressure as a signal that it can supposedly keep fighting, that it can supposedly keep dropping bombs on cities. Different signals are needed.”
The southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia has been a regular target of Russian bombardment with strikes intensifying in the past few months.

On Saturday, a 6-year-old girl was among those killed in Zaporizhzhia when one strike reduced part of an apartment block to rubble. Her grandfather, Anatoliy Chumniy, stood sobbing over her body, laid on the ground in a white bag, after rescuers pulled it from the wreckage.
“Her birthday would have been at the end of the month,” he said through tears.
It was the third mass-casualty attack on Ukraine this week.

Nearly 80 civilians were killed in Russian strikes on Wednesday and Thursday, including at least 30 killed by a bomb in the eastern garrison city of Kramatorsk and 22 others by a missile in the town of Pryluky, about 130 km (80 miles) east of Kyiv.

The diesel deal was also criticized by US lawmakers, including one of Trump’s fellow Republicans, Representative Don Bacon, who said it was time to apply more sanctions that Congress had recently passed, not lift them.
Analysts said the agreement was unlikely to lead to sustained lower fuel prices, with the volumes still much lower than what Russia usually exports when its refineries are not under attack.
Britain vows to strengthen Russia sanctions

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham spoke with Zelenskyy on Saturday and said Britain would strengthen its sanctions on Russia, according to a Downing Street spokesperson, who added that the two leaders would meet in person in the coming days.

The latest strikes followed talks between Ukrainian and European officials with US negotiators in Miami on Friday, which were aimed at developing a common proposal for ending the war, according to a person familiar with the discussions.
Trump announced the diesel deal while the negotiations were under way, a move Zelenskyy said had caught Kyiv by surprise.
The Ukrainian delegation was headed home on Saturday, presidential aide Dmytro Lytvyn was cited by the Interfax Ukraine news agency as saying.
Putin said after a call with Trump on Friday that an immediate resumption of ‌peace ⁠talks was unlikely, citing Ukrainian drone attacks on Moscow.
US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner may visit Moscow within the next two weeks, Russian state news agency TASS reported on Saturday, citing a source.
In his remarks at the White House, Trump criticized Zelenskyy over the lack of a peace deal, while demanding an end to Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy facilities.
“I said to him, ‘Do what you want. Don’t hit refineries. There’s plenty of targets. Don’t hit refineries.’ And he went out and he hit,” Trump said. “He better damn well stop.”
“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals, but for some reason he never does,” he added. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Delhi braces for more protests as 'cockroach' group's leaders released
articles.summary: The leaders, including CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, had been detained when they arrived in Delhi on Saturday.

blocks.text: A court in the Indian capital has ordered the release of top leaders of the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) even as the city braces for protests for a second day with thousands of security personnel deployed and roads barricaded.

Abhijeet Dipke - who began the movement in May after India's Chief Justice likened some jobless young people to "cockroaches" - and other leaders had been detained on arrival in Delhi on Saturday to lead protests seeking electoral reforms.
Police refused them permission to protest and unprecedented curbs were in place to thwart the protesters from reaching the venue.
But thousands did try - media reports said 7,000 were detained and released late at night.
The CJP - which is not registered as a political party in India - is seeking electoral reforms just months before crucial state elections.
It has also demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating voters' lists - which the Election Commission has denied.

On Sunday morning, the CJP lawyer Ratna Singh said she had been informed by the police that Dipke and two other senior CJP leaders - Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka - will be produced before the magistrate by the police seeking their remand "to maintain public peace".

She later posted on X that the three had been set free by the court "on the condition that they will not engage in breach of peace for one year" - it's not clear what that means and whether the CJP leaders can take part in protests.
Saturday saw dramatic developments as police officials boarded the flight to detain Dipke, Das and Ranka as their plane landed.

Police had refused permission for the protest to take place at Jantar Mantar, a landmark in the Indian capital, and the city was in a virtual lockdown to prevent the protesters from reaching the venue.
At least 45 metro stations were shut and Delhi's main railway stations were shut with major train services cancelled. Many protesters attempting to travel from outside were de-boarded en route.
Much of Delhi looked like a city under siege on Saturday, with roads barricaded and offices, shops and restaurants shut.
The day began with expectations of a major gathering at Jantar Mantar, but only a handful of protesters managed to reach the site before police swiftly removed them.
The road that the CJP had occupied for weeks earlier this summer seeking education reforms remained barricaded at both ends, guarded by thousands of police and paramilitary personnel.
The deployment continued through the day, but little happened at the site.
Elsewhere in the city, thousands of protesters still turned up, including activists and senior lawyers who were all detained.
Student leader Neha Bora tried to march from Dilli Haat to Jantar Mantar but was also stopped and taken away. They were all released later on Saturday.
One woman who managed to evade the police and reach Connaught Place told us: "In a democracy, everyone has the right to protest and to say if we are not happy.
"Peaceful protests have been there for ages. We are not living in pre-independent India. We request the government to let us protest."
The CJP has called for more protests on Sunday.
The row centres over a mammoth exercise to update electoral rolls nationwide - the commission has said it's a routine exercise to weed out dead, duplicate or ineligible voters.

At least 130 million voter names have been purged from the rolls so far and in many states, the exercise has been shrouded in controversy, with tens of thousands of people alleging they have been wrongly removed.
The CJP - and opposition parties - accuse Kumar of favouring Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in the way the electoral rolls are being updated.
The Election Commission and the BJP have denied this.
The CJP first emerged as a major protest movement during weeks of demonstrations over the summer demanding education reforms and the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
The group stemmed from a joke made by Dipke in response to a remark by Chief Justice Surya Kant, who had likened jobless youngsters to "cockroaches". He later said the comments were misinterpreted.

Dipke, who previously worked with the opposition Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), had just completed a master's degree at Boston University when he posted a question on X in May: "What if all cockroaches come together?"
The post went viral, and the CJP was born. Momentum built around the movement which tapped into anger over unemployment, exam paper leaks and government accountability.
Their five-week-long protest ended in celebration for the protesters in July after the resignation of India's education minister.

articles.title: Sugarfree’s ‘Dramachine’ gets the classic vinyl treatment
articles.summary: For years, fans have clamored for vinyl releases of Sugarfree’s albums. Their contemporaries have been rolling out remastered editions of their catalogs, and Sugarfree surely deserves the same.

blocks.text: For years, fans have clamored for vinyl releases of Sugarfree’s albums. Their contemporaries have been rolling out remastered editions of their catalogs, and Sugarfree surely deserves the same.

items: Ebe Dancel's 'Baliktanaw' album provided comfort during the pandemic by revisiting his songs from Sugarfree with stripped-down arrangements, focusing on themes of loss and healing.
While Sugarfree's debut album 'Sa Wakas' was released on vinyl, it was criticized for poor sound quality, prompting plans for remastered releases of their next two albums by Backspacer Records.
Jett Galindo, an experienced mastering engineer, is set to improve the sound quality of Sugarfree's albums, ensuring that the emotional dynamics of the music are preserved and enhanced.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

During the pandemic, Ebe Dancel’s Baliktanaw album became a quiet companion for many of us. Dancel revisited the songs he wrote for his former band Sugarfree, stripping the arrangements to acoustic guitar, keyboards, and strings. The songs, and Dancel’s earnest vocals, soothed the ache of disconnection, of loss and longing, while the world stayed home.

Sugarfree never claimed the title of patron band of loss and longing. The bands that came before them and their own contemporaries also wrote about heartbreak, approaching the difficult topic with irony, anger, novelty, or social commentary, usually with big, audacious gestures. Dancel went small.

His songs are confessional monologues: plainspoken, conversational, raw. They hang on small details that put you in a specific time and place. They leave you with a feeling that is hard to shake. Listen to the tender “Tulog Na,” or the grief that fills a messy room of memories in “Kwarto.” Dancel’s best songs, however, do not stand in place. They never wallow in grief. There is always movement in them, a search for healing, a step past the hurt.

The band’s debut, “Sa Wakas,” did make it to vinyl, and it was a letdown. The sibilance hisses, the sound is muddy, and the dynamics are flattened. It sounds like an album that went direct to vinyl without anyone stopping to master it for the format.

That major oversight is being corrected. Indie OPM label Backspacer Records is releasing the band’s next two albums on vinyl: Dramachine and Tala-Arawan. The vinyl masters are by Jett Galindo, and the choice is perfect.

Galindo grew up in Quezon City and earned a psychology degree from the Ateneo before leaving for Berklee to study audio engineering. In 2013, she became the assistant to legendary cutter Doug Sax at The Mastering Lab in Ojai, California. Sax founded the first independent mastering studio in 1967, and Galindo calls him “the grandfather of mastering.” He taught her to cut vinyl.

She then spent nearly a decade at The Bakery, a mastering house on the Sony Pictures lot where she mastered and cut vinyl for Green Day’s Revolution Radio, the La La Land soundtrack, and Billie Eilish’s Hit Me Hard and Soft. Her credits also include Barbra Streisand, Weezer, Pink Floyd, and Neil Young. She now runs her own studio, Jett Galindo Mastering, in Los Angeles.

What she brings to Sugarfree is her mentor’s creed: less is more, and stay faithful to the music. She also knows the format’s traps. In interviews, she has named the hazards that make vinyl cutting tricky, and sibilance tops the list. That is the very flaw that sank Sa Wakas.

I heard a test pressing of Dramachine, and the difference is immediate. The soft-loud dynamics, the album’s emotional driver, are intact and in balance. The quiet passages breathe, and the loud ones land without flattening everything around them. The clarity puts Dancel’s voice where it belongs, front and center, every word legible. This is how a classic album should sound.

It has been a busy year for Backspacer. Since its first OPM release during the pandemic, the self-titled album of indie darling Peryodiko, the label has collected a string of Awit Awards and earned the respect of vinyl collectors for its design, packaging, and mastering. Its catalog now includes emerging acts, legacy pop singers, P-pop superstars, and elder statesmen of rock and jazz.

Robert Tuazon, who runs the label with his wife Tasha, talks about the work like a fan, not a businessman. “As music fans, this gives us the ultimate pride and satisfaction,” he said in an early interview with this writer. “So as long as we can accommodate them, we would love to keep continuing to press more and more OPM records on vinyl.”
That leaves one piece of unfinished business. Tuazon is hoping for a second crack at Sa Wakas, with Galindo at the board.
I say give it to them. The album that started it all deserves to sound like the classic that it is. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Winner in life: Carlos Yulo ready to take on new challenges
articles.summary: Even after completing his golden collection, Carlos Yulo has no plans to slow down anytime soon, pursuing not only success in gymnastics but also opportunities to grow and develop as an individual

blocks.text: WINNER. Carlos Yulo in action for the Philippines in the 2026 Asian Games.
Edgar Su/Reuters
Even after completing his golden collection, Carlos Yulo has no plans to slow down anytime soon, pursuing not only success in gymnastics but also opportunities to grow and develop as an individual
MANILA, Philippines – Carlos Yulo has nothing more to prove.

He has won gold medals in almost every major competition, capturing two at the Olympics, three at the World Championships, 12 at the Asian Championships, five in the World Cup Series, nine at the Southeast Asian Games, and, most recently, two at the Asian Games to complete his collection.
And yet, Yulo has no plans to slow down anytime soon. He continues to chase success in gymnastics while looking for opportunities to grow as an individual.

“There’s always more to improve on, more challenges to take on, and more to learn. God gives us unlimited challenges and we really have to embrace them. If His blessings are also unlimited, why should we hold back when it comes to giving our best to ourselves and, of course, to Him? For me, it’s really all about gaining experiences,” said Yulo in a mix of Filipino and English.

“It doesn’t matter how many times I fall or how many times I lose. Even when I was younger, winning was never really the main goal — it’s the experiences we gain in life that we carry with us as we grow older.”

blocks.caption: Winner in life: Carlos Yulo ready to take on new challenges

blocks.text: After the Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, Yulo immediately returned to training. He, his younger brother Eldrew, and Juancho Miguel Besana are training in Antibes, France, for the World Championships in Rotterdam, Netherlands, from October 17 to 25.

Although he has won titles across major competitions, the 26-year-old looks to defend a world title for the first time in his career. He is eyeing another gold following his vault triumph at the 2025 World Championships in Jakarta, Indonesia, where he also won bronze in floor exercise.
Yulo also has his sights set on the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, where he is the defending champion in both the floor exercise and vault.

“There’s still a lot,” said Yulo when asked what more he wants to achieve. “Of course, the Olympics will always be one of them. And when my gymnastics career comes to an end — which I think is still quite a long way off — I really want to help young children by giving them the proper knowledge about gymnastics and sharing my experiences, both from my career and from my journey through life. I really want to give back to them.”
“I hope that one day, we’ll see many Filipino gymnasts competing internationally.”
Beyond his gymnastics aspirations, Yulo is also entering an important new chapter in his life as he prepares to marry his longtime girlfriend, Chloe San Jose.
Yulo proposed to San Jose in December 2025, but they kept their engagement private until shortly after his golden double at the Asian Games, when they decided to announce it publicly.
Sure, juggling wedding preparations while staying focused on his gymnastics will not be easy, but it is anew journey that Yulo is embracing with open arms.

“I’m always happy to take on these challenges in my life. It’s not going to be always smooth. I’m really, really happy and grateful for whatever challenges the Lord gives me, and I think this is one of His challenges for me. I feel like I’m not alone because I have so many people who love me,” said Yulo.

At the heart of his support system is San Jose, whom Yulo credits as one of the people who helped propel him to success. His decision to give her two engagement rings, symbolizing his two Olympic gold medals, reflects the significance of their relationship and the place she holds in his life.
“I didn’t just win in sports; I also won in life,” Yulo said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: US justice department investigates TV networks over Trump pool coverage
articles.summary: The White House had blocked access for CNN, MS Now and Politico, leading them to restrict pool coverage.

blocks.text: The US justice department (DoJ) has said it is investigating several TV networks over whether they broke federal competition laws when they recently suspended pool coverage of President Donald Trump.
Last month, five networks paused their presidential coverage for several days in response to the Trump administration withdrawing the credentials of reporters from CNN, MS Now and Politico.

The justice department asked ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News to hand over communications related to the pool and said that the boycott could violate the Sherman Act, referring to a law that bars companies from engaging in monopolistic business practices.
Pool members usually share their material with the wider media.
A DoJ spokesperson said: "The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these ​news organisations have violated the antitrust laws."
The television networks have not yet commented.
Trump blocked CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House last month after accusing the organisations of writing "fiction or lies" about his team.
The White House later reinstated their access after a ruling from a judge. The three outlets had sued the Trump administration, arguing the restricted access violated their First Amendment rights.

The First Amendment forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press - language that courts have traditionally interpreted as preventing the government from discriminating against the media based on the content of their coverage.
The Trump administration has taken a number of legal actions against news publications in the US, including lawsuits over coverage of the president.
In February, the White House announced it was taking control of the press pool which has access to Trump and had for more than a century been managed by the White House Correspondents' Association.

The same month, the Trump administration moved to bar Associated Press (AP) reporters and photographers from spaces where access is limited, such as the Oval Office or Air Force One, because of the outlet's usage of the term "Gulf of Mexico" instead of "Gulf of America". AP filed a lawsuit and the case remains ongoing.
